News.title: Milei’s Falklands rant should be urgent warning to Labour to properly arm our troops & protect ALL Brits here and abroad
News.content:
Falk in the road

OUR new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted he is “unwavering” about keeping the Falklands British.

Such a statement from a strong, principled Government backed by a powerful military should leave the Argies thinking twice about ever trying again to take what they call “Las Malvinas”.



Instead, Argentinian president Javier Milei smells weakness and decline. Like our enemies in Russia and China, he knows Britain’s Armed Forces have been hollowed out for years and most of our warships and subs are broken.

Milei will also have read depressing reports that the funding crisis is so bad that Army exercises have been scrapped.



Most of all, Milei knows Labour’s utter failure to ramp up defence spending has caused a bitter rift with our closest ally.

Donald Trump now publicly questions why he should back Britain over the Falklands when Keir Starmer refused to offer any help over the war on Iran.



The US — increasingly close to Argentina over oil — now sees the UK as an unreliable military partner.

For now, the only reason Argentina has confined itself to sabre-rattling is that its army is so small it probably wouldn’t be able to overwhelm British forces already stationed on the Falklands.

But that is no reason for complacency.

Or the time for weasel words from treacherous Foreign Office mandarins like former Permanent Secretary Lord McDonald, who suggested to the BBC yesterday the islands were too far away, too costly and too strategically unimportant to be worth the £500million-a-year cost of defending them.



No doubt Miliband is receiving similar advice from the Whitehall appeasers who persuaded Andy Burnham and Starmer to give away the Chagos Islands.

But the fact that craven politicians have left Britain with virtually no chance today of sending a Falklands task force of the size sent by Margaret Thatcher in 1982 is NOT a reason for more capitulation.

Milei’s rant should be yet another urgent warning to Labour to arm our military properly and protect ALL British citizens at home and abroad.

Not so slick

AS WITH so much from our new Prime Minister, the promise fails to meet the reality.

On the face of it, there is good news that he will finally approve drilling in the Jackdaw North Sea gas field — a sensible decision that Labour should have taken two years ago.



But in hock to the Net Zero loons, Burnham is still likely to block the Rosebank development because that contains mainly oil.

Norway has sunk 45 North Sea wells while Labour has delayed.

Britain needs BOTH to be operational as soon as possible AND to start exploration of new reserves.

Anything less will leave our energy security in as much of a mess as ever.

News.title: Why it’s party over for Reform after latest saga – unless Nigel Farage can get a grip
News.content:
NIGEL Farage came pretty close to throwing in the towel this summer.

Seething about his family getting dragged into politics and shaken by threats and a torrent of abuse, he mooted packing it all in and going fishing.



The brutal murder of his colleague Ann Widdecombe could have rightly broken even the bravest of leaders, and it almost did after what I understand were tense talks with those closest to him.

Friends talk darkly about chilling information soon to enter the public domain that will shock even the Reform leader’s most ardent haters.



A chink of light at his inner thoughts was clear in some interviews where he couldn’t quite bring himself to say he actually wanted to be the PM.

But whether it was his sense of duty or ambition — or frankly just a love of the game — he hit the stump in Clacton instead and vowed to keep buggering on.

This weekend’s party conference was supposed to be the reset moment, where after the Starmer-destroying highs of 2025, Reform could put a summer of squabbles and wobbles behind them and actually focus on the policy.

In nearly 20 years of covering the man, Birmingham’s jamboree was on course to be the most professional gathering of his true believers that I had ever seen.

Corporate Britain was out in force, as were the big global firms, noses pressed against the glass, desperate to read the runes of a Reform government.

What would have been considered crackers just 18 months ago remains a moonshot chance: Nigel Farage, PM.



Though with exhibitors and power suits aplenty, like so many Farage-adjacent events there was still always a sense of the absurd.

Anyone lucky enough to remember the manic days of Ukip knows that more often or not, their events descended into carnivals of chaos.

So despite the veneer of professionalism, slick carpet and shiny signs, there remained a whiff of carnage — an unshakeable feeling things could go t*ts up at any moment.



There are more pyrotechnics on the stage these days, but it was always the fireworks elsewhere that caused the real scenes.

And so it came to pass. Once chastised by chin-stroking pundits for being too loyal to allies he should have cut loose, the axe swung at two in the morning.

After initially branding Channel 4’s Thursday night exposé a “hoax”, it became clear in the small hours that the damage could be mortal after a long summer of sleaze stories.

Long-term aide and part-time honorary son Dan Jukes was jettisoned after walking straight into a trap sprung by climate change activists posing as deep-pocketed foreign donors looking to bend the donation rules.

One too many negronis seems to have put paid to the political career of policy chief James Orr, who was seen slurring his way out of a job by promising a fake millionaire the world.



Now Reform can rage about it all being a globalist plot, and a co-ordinated deep-state stitch-up, a sophisticated attempt to bury them by their terrified establishment enemies.

And they probably have a point to some degree — the gloves are certainly off.

But they should know by now that this torrent was coming, and in asking to not just lead the country, but blow up half a century of political consensus, that it was part of the package.

They have been warned enough times by supporters and critical friends that the scrutiny was coming, whether it feels fair or not when the heat is on.

Though you might not know it from the airwaves, there was some serious meat from Reform yesterday.



A potential referendum on the House of Lords, ripping up how the judiciary is appointed and remarkable accord with the man likely to be France’s next PM that would see the French finally accept the return of small boat crossers.

But yet again all blown out of the water by entirely avoidable scandal.

This latest saga must be a reckoning for Reform — get a grip or give over to their claim to be the dominant force on the Right.

Despite the love in the hall, Farage felt the need to spell out to his adoring fans: “I am determined to lead Reform at the next election.”

And his problem is he may well get that wish sooner rather than later.



The odds of an early General Election have shortened dramatically in the last 48 hours.

With Reform beset by fresh chaos, a new wave of investigations and another bout of dire headlines about money, Andy Burnham may soon be laughing all the way to the Palace.

After Keir Starmer’s steaming leaving present on No10’s doorstep, if Labour can see off Wacko Zacko Polanski in the upcoming Holborn and St Pancras by-election, the case to go to the country will become irresistible.

The Left semi united, the Right deeply riven with a visceral loathing and mutual suspicion.

Worst-case scenario for Burnham, dopey Ed Davey has made clear with his slobbering all over the new PM that he’s open to doing business.



And that really would be a disaster for a country in desperate need of actual reform.

ED MILIBAND has been very tight-lipped about Chagos since taking over at the Foreign Office.

But that’s unlikely to survive the first big contact between the new government and Donald Trump later this month at the United Nations in New York.

The botched plan to pay Mauritius to take over our overseas territory in the Indian Ocean was dead in the water after the Americans scotched it over fears they would lose access to a vital airbase.



But now fresh efforts by the Foreign Office to resurrect the surrender deal have left Washington baffled.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Not least because at a time when Britain is in uproar over threats to the Falkland Islands – even while asking the Americans to slap down new Argie sabre-rattling – our government seems so willing to give up other territory willy nilly.

My mole says things are set to come to a head again when the new PM heads Stateside in a few weeks’ time.

News.title: Reform UK conference LIVE: Nigel Farage says ‘campaign of attacks’ won't distract Reform as speech descends into chaos
News.content:
Nigel Farage has finally addressed allegations the party knowingly accepted foreign donations to pay for polls that weren't declared, before speaking at Reform UK's conference

Nigel Farage says Reform won’t be distracted by ‘campaign of attacks’ in his speech at the Reform UK conference tonight.

Mr Farage took to the main stage at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham to give his speech this evening, during which he was interrupted numerous times by protesters and hecklers.

The party leader said: “We have been the subject of a highly co-ordinated campaign of attacks.” He added: “But I promise you, we will not be distracted by any of this. We are absolutely determined in what we’re doing.”

The annual gathering has gone off the rails after explosive allegations over foreign donations saw two high-profile aides forced to step down. Comms chief Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr were recorded allegedly plotting for a foreign donor to pay £32,500 for off-the-books polling on behalf of the party, in a potential breach of electoral law.

Meanwhile, Mr Farage has insisted Reform UK has “broken no laws” and had not “taken any dodgy money” amid allegations the party breached political donation rules. Foreign companies are not a permissible source of funding for parties, including for payments for studies and research, and accepting donations from them could constitute a criminal offence.

The Reform party conference is due to continue tomorrow, but here's everything you need to know so far...

News.title: Primark issues urgent recall as shoppers told to 'stop using item immediately'
News.content:
Primark issues urgent recall as shoppers told to 'stop using item immediately'

Shoppers who purchased the item have been urged to stop using it 'immediately' and return it to any branch for a full refund as it could pose health risks

View 2 Images Shoppers have been urged to stop using the product immediately

Primark has urgently recalled a fashion accessory after it was found to contain a chemical that could pose health risks.

Shoppers who purchased the item have been urged to stop using it "immediately" and return it to any branch for a full refund - without the need for a receipt.

Primark's 101 Dalmatians Zip Purse, part of its Disney collection, "has been found to contain phthalates above permitted levels," a recall notice reads. "This may cause harm to health and the environment."

‌



Phthalates, synthetic chemicals used to make plastics softer and more flexible, can pose health risks to children as well as potentially damaging the reproductive system if present in excessive quantities.

View 2 Images Primark said the purse contained a chemical which 'may cause harm to health and the environment' (Image: Primark)

The faux leather purse was therefore found not to meet the retailer’s usual high safety standards. The product was sold in UK stores between March 2026 and June 2026.

Primark has also asked the public to spread the word about the recall, “especially if you know that the recalled product was offered, borrowed or sold to someone else.”

The recall notice reads: "We are recalling our product pictured above due to a safety issue. Model: 101 Dalmatians Faux Leather Coin Purse (Kimball no. 2595301).

"This was sold in Primark stores in the UK between March 2026 and June 2026.

‌



"We've learned the product does not meet our usual high safety standards. The product has been found to contain phthalates above permitted levels, and this may cause harm to health and the environment.

"Please stop using the product immediately. Please return the product to any of our Primark stores. It is not necessary to show proof of purchase. The returned product will be fully refunded.

"We apologise for any inconvenience and concerns this may cause."

Customers seeking more information about the recall have been asked to email help.uk@help.primark.com.

News.title: Sainsbury’s recalls popular food item over health risk as ‘do not eat’ warning issued
News.content:
Sainsbury’s recalls popular food item over health risk as ‘do not eat’ warning issued

The Food Standards Agency has warned shoppers not to eat the recalled Sainsbury’s product after listeria was found.

View 2 Images Sainsbury’s has issued an urgent recall for a popular food item, with shoppers warned not to eat it. (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Sainsbury’s has issued an urgent recall for a popular food item, with shoppers warned not to eat it.

‌



The supermarket is recalling its Inspired to Cook Pitted Black Olives after Listeria monocytogenes was found in the product, a ccording to the Food Standards Agency.

‌



The recall affects 120g packs with use-by dates of September 6, September 7 and September 10, 2026.

‌



Customers who have bought an affected pack have been told not to eat the olives and instead return them to their nearest Sainsbury’s store for a full refund.

View 2 Images Sainsbury’s is recalling its Inspired to Cook Pitted Black Olives

‌



The FSA said symptoms caused by Listeria monocytogenes can be similar to flu and may include a high temperature, muscle aches or pain, chills, feeling or being sick and diarrhoea.

In rare cases, the infection can become more severe and lead to serious complications such as meningitis.

Some people are particularly vulnerable to listeria infections, including those aged over 65, pregnant women and their unborn babies, babies under one month old and people with weakened immune systems.

Article continues below

Sainsbury’s will display point-of-sale notices in stores selling the affected product explaining the recall and what customers should do.

No proof of purchase is required for customers returning the recalled olives for a full refund.

Anyone seeking further information can visit the Sainsbury’s website or contact its careline on 0800 028 8303.

News.title: ‘Much-loved’ boy, 12, who died in Co Mayo train crash pictured as tributes pour in
News.content:
‘Much-loved’ boy, 12, who died in Co Mayo train crash pictured as tributes pour in

Eoin Doyle, 12, tragically died after a train collided with a car at a level crossing in Kiltybo, near Ballyhaunis in Co Mayo, Ireland, on Thursday evening

View Image Eoin Doyle, 12, died at the scene of the crash in Co Mayo

A "much-loved" 12-year-old boy who died after a train crashed into a car in Ireland has been pictured for the first time.

‌



Eoin Doyle was involved in the collision at a level crossing in Kiltybo, near Ballyhaunis in Co Mayo on Thursday, September 3.

‌



Emergency services raced to the location shortly after 8.45pm, but the youngster was tragically pronounced dead at the scene.

‌



A man in his late 40s was rushed to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Tributes have since poured in for Eoin following the tragedy. His death notice read: "The death has occurred of Eoin Doyle, Gurrane, Ballyhaunis- tragically following an accident on 3rd September 2026.

"Deeply regretted by his heartbroken parents Declan and Elaine (née Corcoran) and his twin sister Saoirse, step-brother Conor, grandparents Pat and Marguerite Doyle and Ger and Mary Corcoran, uncles, aunts, cousins, relatives and friends."

‌



Eoin's funeral will take place on September 8 at St. Patrick's Church in Cloonfad before a burial at Ballyhaunis Cemetery.

A local sports club attended by the youngster described him as a "much loved member of our underage teams."

The Ballyhaunis GAA Club added that Eoin was "a talented young footballer and, above all, a wonderful young boy who was a great friend and teammate to so many within our club."

‌



Aontú deputy and Mayo TD Paul Lawless, who lives close to the scene of the collision, said the whole community has been shocked and deeply saddened by the loss.

"We have yet to hear the details, but it would seem to be a horrible freak accident," deputy Lawless said.

"I can't recall such a fatal crash on a rail line ever happening here before. It is very rare in Ireland. It is heartbreaking to think this lad was at the start of his young life, coming home from training and with everything ahead of him.

‌



"I believe he had only recently had the joy of seeing the Sam Maguire when Mayo captain Jack Coyne brought it to Ballyhaunis GAA club.

"To think his life was snatched away in such a tragic way is horrifying. We are all thinking of his family and his father who is in hospital after the accident."

Deputy Lawless said the crossing, which is around the corner from him, is among others in the area that are "very rural" and "not automated."

‌



He said: "It can be little more than traffic lights with gates that users open and shut and can be confusing, for example, for motorists who may not be familiar with it."

Lawless called for a full review of safeguards and an investigation to establish what happened.

The line was closed overnight and for the majority of Friday while Gardai conducted a technical examination of the scene. It reopened shortly after 4pm, reports the Irish Mirror.

‌



It comes as Irish Rail Chief Executive Mary Considine said a full investigation into the incident is underway as she expressed her sympathies to Eoin's family.

"On behalf of Iarnród Éireann. I wish to express our sincerest sympathies to the family of the young boy who tragically lost his life in Ballyhaunis last night," Ms Considine said. "Incidents like these are extremely difficult for all involved.

"I would also like to convey my sincere appreciation to all those who responded with such professionalism and care at the scene, both the emergency services, An Garda Síochána and our own staff.

‌



"A full investigation into the incident is underway and further details will become clear as the investigation continues. We appreciate the understanding and cooperation of our customers at this time.

"Our thoughts remain with the family, friends and wider community in Ballyhaunis and with everyone affected by this tragic incident."

Gardai are continuing to appeal for information following the fatal crash.

Article continues below

"Road users and pedestrians with camera footage (including dash-cam) who were in the area of Kiltybo, Ballyhaunis, Co. Mayo, on Thursday 3rd September 2026 between 8.15pm and 9.15pm are asked to make this footage available to investigating Gardaí," a statement said.

"Anyone with any information is asked to contact Ballina Garda Station on (096) 20560, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station."

News.title: 'Shameless Nigel Farage is the bad boss from hell and a cynical con man, heading a poisonous Reform'
News.content:
Infamy, infamy - they’ve all got it in for me.

Tetchy Nigel Farage mutating into a hapless Kenneth Williams in the latest episode of the Carry On Reform farce leaves most voters jeering at a dodgy trickster going backwards, not forwards, to Downing Street.

The mocking Greenpeace banner delaying his heckler-interrupted big speech, under-powered by his standards, symbolised a Hard-Right party losing control, reeling under scrutiny, Farage’s mini-Trump tribute act past its sell-by date with Donald of Iran bombing here. Reform zealots in Birmingham saluting their leader are on another planet in believing the latest financial scandal to engulf the party was a hoax or doesn’t matter, wild-eyed conspiracy theorists screaming they’re victims of conspiracies.

View 5 Images Farage dismissed the undercover sting as a "little local difficulty" (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Should Nigel Farage resign as Reform UK leader? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

Shameless Farage, a career politician who cons and tricks the public by forever portraying himself as the persecuted outsider, is the bad boss from hell sacrificing two of his closest, most important aides, Dan Dukes and James Orr, to save his own skin over what Nasty Nige disingenuously dismissed as a "little local difficulty” and “loose pub talk”.

The filmed cosy private chat over oysters and wine confirmed that Reform is a sleazy, poisonous and, mercifully, amateur organisation. Operation Save Nigel after the claims of dodgily-funded opinion polls and discussion of what would be illegal foreign donations will repel curious floating voters already deserting a leader and party leaking support - one recent survey even putting them in third place behind Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives as well as Andy Burnham’s revived Labour.

View 5 Images Nigel Farage branded protesters as "boring" during his conference speech (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

Farage attempting to project confidence, signing a phantom migrant returns agreement with Far-Right French hate-monger Jordan Bardella, a statement not worth the giant card it was printed on when both aren’t in power, may well hide inner turmoil and doubt.

‌



Beating a bin in a farcical Clacton by-election he called proved both humiliating, Farage skipping the declaration, and resolved absolutely nothing - but did underline his judgement is flawed. The Westminster inquiry into his secret personal £5million 'bung' resumed and wasn’t scuppered, and could yet trigger a second, real contest.

View 5 Images Several people brought Farage's speech to a pause (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

Farage may face another over expensive unregistered housing, drivers, security and social media punting from aristo wealthy benefactor and convicted fraudster “Posh George” Cottrell. Then there is the police investigation into £500,000 donated to Reform by Posh George’s blue-blood mother Fiona Cottrell and the origin of that money in what could prove the most explosive ticking time bomb.

View 5 Images Nigel Farage was interrupted numerous times during his Reform UK conference speech (Image: AP Photo/Thomas Krych)

‌



No wonder wannabes in the Reform hierarchy mutter serial quitter Farage could chuck his toys out of the pram again, petulantly resigning to spend more time with other people’s money, as his Prime Minister dream turns into a nightmare.

View 5 Images 'Reform works for billionaires' banner raised by heckler (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

Super rich Reform banker Zia Yusuf and Tory turncoat Robert Jenrick appear to think so by running what sound and look like undeclared leadership campaigns to fill a vacancy.

Momentum is vital in politics and Farage is stuck in reverse, a conference supposed to be a relaunch pad showing he and Reform remain in a hole and are still digging.

News.title: Reform plunged into chaos by donations row as Nigel Farage heckled during major speech
News.content:
Reform plunged into chaos by donations row as Nigel Farage heckled during major speech

Two top aides to Nigel Farage were forced to step down following an undercover sting, which appeared to show the pair discussing how to disguise donations from foreign donors

Hecklers kicked out of Farage speech at Reform Conference

Reform was plunged into turmoil last night(FRI) as Scotland Yard said it was assessing reports that senior figures sought to evade electoral law over donations.

‌



Two top aides to Nigel Farage were forced to step down following an undercover sting, which appeared to show the pair discussing how to disguise donations from foreign donors.

‌



Long-standing aide Dan Jukes and policy chief James Orr left their posts, pending an internal probe, as the donations scandal threatened to engulf the party. They all deny wrongdoing.

‌



Labour and the Liberal Democrats reported Reform to the police over a report, by Channel 4 News and undercover group Verbatim, which aired on the eve of the party's annual conference.

But Mr Farage sought to downplay the secretly-recorded comments as "loose pub talk" as he addressed delegates in a chaotic speech beset by hecklers and delays.

View 7 Images Farage emerged to fanfare and pyrotechnics (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

‌



He complained to party faithful that Reform had been “the subject of a highly co-ordinated campaign of attacks” by the establishment around the main parties.

Mr Farage added: “Reform has broken no law. We take compliance extremely seriously. And ask yourself, why is all of this happening? Anyone got a clue why it’s happening? Because they’re scared of us. That’s why it’s happening.”

‌



Reform faces the possibility of probes by the police and the Electoral Commission over the allegations thrown up by the year-long undercover investigation.

View 7 Images Nigel Farage's keynote speech was interrupted four times (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

The footage appeared to show Mr Jukes and Mr Orr seek to orchestrate funds from journalists posing as a wealthy American and his UK-based son. This included £32,500 for polls that made the front pages news, which Reform had allegedly commissioned.

‌



In a meeting over oysters and wine in Clacton in July, Mr Farage was filmed celebrating the results of polls, saying it provided “bang for buck,” adding: “It worked. Boom."

There was also allegedly a discussion of whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, which is against the law.

View 7 Images The Reform leader chanted "boring, boring" when a protester interrupted him (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

‌



Foreign companies are not a permissible source of funding for parties, and accepting donations from them could constitute a criminal offence.

A Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: “We’re aware of media reporting on Thursday, 3 September involving political party donations and an alleged breach of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 relating to polling.

Richard Tice humiliated by protest banner on stage before Nigel Farage speech

‌



"We will assess this matter and any information provided to us.” The force has not launched an investigation at this stage.

The Electoral Commission said: "We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met Police."

View 7 Images He was forced to move through the crowd before his speech, due to a security issue (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Legal expert Joshua Rozenberg said the Political Parties Elections and Referendums Act 2000 makes it an offence to facilitate donations to a party by anybody other than a permissible donor.

He told the BBC: "If you do something to enable your party to get money from somebody who is not permitted to pay that to your party, and you do that knowingly, or if you give information to the treasurer, then you are committing a criminal offence.”

The row dominated Reform's annual conference in Birmingham, where Mr Farage had been hoping to get on the front foot again after intense scrutiny over his finances.

‌



View 7 Images One protester was seen running up the aisle toward the stage (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

But in further drama, Mr Farage's big speech to party faithful was delayed due to security concerns after a stunt by activists disrupted a speech by his deputy Richard Tice.

Greenpeace activists deployed a remote-controlled banner depicting Mr Farage as the Monopoly man, carrying a sack of cash, with the slogan "Collect £5 million, burn the planet".

‌



Nigel Farage makes theatrical entrance for conference speech

Security officials searched under the stage with a search dog before Mr Farage finally took to the stage.

Several climate activists were then dragged out by security, after unfurling banners saying 'REFORM WORKS FOR BILLIONAIRES' and shouting "Nigel! You're bankrolled by billionaires!"

‌



View 7 Images Numerous climate activists were manhandled out of the room (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

One of the protesters thrown out of Nigel Farage's speech said he had stood up to highlight corruption at the heart of Reform. The heckler, named Ed, told The Mirror he is part of a group called Resist Reform.

He said: "We just stood up in the Reform conference to highlight the corruption at the heart of the Reform Party." He added: "So the idea was to raise people's awareness of that and to show that that's happening, because they talk a lot about nation and community values in that room.

‌



View 7 Images Nigel Farage's conference speech was interrupted by protesters in a day of chaos for Reform (Image: AP Photo/Thomas Krych)

"And I believe some of the people there are genuinely there because that's what they believe, but they should know that this is a party that will flout the rules to get into power, and that just doesn't really care about the kinds of things that would keep us as ordinary citizens that we would actually have to obey."

Mr Jukes described the report as "entrapment over a prolonged period", claiming the reporters were foreign funded climate activists. He said in a statement: "I totally deny any wrongdoing but have stepped back from politics in order to clear my name."

Article continues below

Mr Orr told Sky News: "I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation into the conduct of the programme, with which I will cooperate fully."

News.title: Lindsay Clancy mistrial declared after jury deadlocks over deaths of her three children
News.content:
Lindsay Clancy mistrial declared after jury deadlocks over deaths of her three children

Lindsay Clancy’s trial has ended in a mistrial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict over the deaths of her three young children.

View 4 Images A mistrial has been declared in the case of Lindsay Clancy (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

A mistrial has been declared in the case of Lindsay Clancy after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict over the deaths of her three children.

Clancy was accused of strangling her three children Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan at their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, in January 2023, before jumping from a second-floor window.

The former labour and delivery nurse, now 36, was left paralysed from the fall and attended the trial in a wheelchair. She had sent her husband, Patrick, out to run errands before he returned home to find the children dead in the basement.

Jurors spent more than 38 hours deliberating before telling the court for a third time that they were unable to reach a unanimous decision.

View 4 Images A mistrial has been declared in the case of Lindsay Clancy (Image: Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledge)

Judge William Sullivan told the jury: “At this point, I'm going to declare that the jury is deadlocked, and I'm going to declare a mistrial,” before discharging them.

Clancy’s mental state at the time of the killings became the central issue during the trial.

Her defence argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible for her children’s deaths, while prosecutors argued she had deliberately killed the three youngsters.

Clancy has not denied killing her children, but pleaded not guilty to three counts of first-degree murder.

The trial heard evidence from more than 80 witnesses and saw around 300 exhibits presented to the jury.

Clancy's attorneys, while defending her, had never rejected her role in the killings.

View 4 Images Defense attorney Kevin Reddington, who represented Lindsay Clancy as her trial ended in a mistrial. (Image: Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledge)

Putting forth a defence of insanity, they argued that Clancy had hallucinations and delusions after giving birth to her youngest child.

They pointed to treatment for mental health problems, adding that she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital just days before the deaths.

Prosecutors, meanwhile, argued Clancy made a calculated decision to intentionally kill her children. They allege that at the time, Clancy sent Patrick out on errands so that he would not be home.

Patrick, who has since remarried, told the court about Lindsay’s declining mental health following the birth of their youngest son, with the "big spiral" starting around a month before the killings.

View 4 Images Judge William Sullivan, who declared a mistrial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict in Lindsay Clancy’s case. (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time," he said.

Patrick said she had intermittently sought help from doctors and had been taking various medications.

He also told jurors he recalled her saying she was beginning to have thoughts of suicide.

The jury had previously told Judge William Sullivan it was struggling to reach a unanimous decision before returning without a verdict for a third time.

Article continues below

Judge Sullivan said: "I’m going to declare a mistrial at this point," before Clancy’s defence asked for the declaration to be temporarily stayed while it sought emergency relief from a higher court.

News.title: 'Nigel Farage's Reform UK conference disaster was up there with Theresa May losing her voice'
News.content:
'Nigel Farage's Reform UK conference disaster was up there with Theresa May losing her voice'

"No end of sacrificial lambs would be enough to keep Reform's Birmingham bash on the rails. They gamely tried to carry on, but it was all anyone was talking about - and the mood among delegates has been suitably glum"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Nigel Farage's motley crew of Reform UK characters aren't often lost for words. But they all quickly clammed up when the Mirror asked them about the party's latest donor drama.

‌



The party dismissed Channel 4's sting as a hoax and a distraction - but less than 12 hours later it was serious enough for them to launch an investigation and for two very senior figures in Farage's orbit to step down.

‌



So desperate was Farage to avoid his flashy conference being derailed, he threw one of his longest-serving and closest aides, Dan Jukes, under the bus - dismissing him as a "contractor".

‌



But no end of sacrificial lambs would be enough to keep Reform's Birmingham bash on the rails. They gamely tried to carry on, but it was all anyone was talking about - and the mood among delegates has been suitably glum.

And all that was before the repeated interruptions of Farage's droning speech by climate protesters. An automatic banner poking fun at Farage's £5m gift unfurled itself at the back of the stage during deputy leader Richard Tice's speech too - presumably intended for the leader's address, but thwarted by the programme running spectacularly late.

As party conference disasters go, it was right up there with Theresa May's lost voice, disintegrating backdrop and being handed a P45 by a comedian.

‌



And there's still one more day of chaos to go on Saturday. Whatever next?

Trump backs chainsaw-weilding madman over Britain in Falklands row

Donald Trump is on the verge of torpedoing America's Special Relationship with Britain and rowing in behind a chainsaw-wielding madman.

The increasingly petty US President has signalled he could stand back and let Argentina try and take back the Falkland Islands.

‌



The madman in question is Javier Milei, Argentina's flamboyant President. Aside from his fondness for waving around a chainsaw, Milei is best known for launching vile attacks on Pope Benedict.

And why is Trump siding with Milei over America's greatest ally? Because Keir Starmer refused to follow him into his Iran war folly.

The Falklands are significantly better defended now than they were in 1982. Should Argentina make a move for them, it will probably be brief and fruitless.

Article continues below

Timeless Dolly back in the charts

How wonderful to see Dolly Parton continue to make history even in death. A week on from her passing, her singles 9 to 5, Jolene and Islands in the Stream have rocketed back into the charts - the first time she's ever had three of the top 10. Her timeless songs will no doubt keep finding new fans for decades to come.

News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a fatal crash which killed seven people including two police officers.

In her first sit-down interview since the A66 crash, speaking exclusively to the BBC, Victoria Fuller said the force needed to become part of a larger force with greater resources.

She said her officers are dealing with some of the highest crime levels in the country akin to those faced by metropolitan forces, but with less than half the number of officers.

Multiple people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.

A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

At the same time, Fuller said Cleveland Police had experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fueling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy murder case, after jury deadlocks
News.content:
The mistrial came after six weeks of court proceedings and after jurors deliberated for more than 40 hours over seven days.

"There will be no decisions made today," Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said on Friday on what could happen next in the case.

He said he would meet with the rest of their legal team to decide whether they will pursue a new trial.

"The facts are Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and the evidence suggested to us that she was in control of her actions when she committed those homicides," he said.

Outside the court on Friday, Reddington said he believed 11 of the 12 jurors would have delivered a verdict that favoured Clancy, had it not been for the one holdout.

But it remains unclear what position any member of the jury took or what talks looked like in the deliberation room.

For weeks the case gripped the country and sparked debate over the topic of postpartum psychosis. Many followed along with livestreams of the trial, as family members and experts testified. Each day, more than 200 members of the media crowded the court and groups of supporters in varying sizes often gathered outside.

The widespread attention even spurred comments on Friday from US President Donald Trump, who called the case a "horrible tragedy".

"She did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse," he said at the White House. "I assume there's going to be another trial."

"But you'll find out what the price to pay is," Trump added. "There'll be a price."

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.

In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

News.title: Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges
News.content:
In his speech, which was light on new policy announcements, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".

He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.

If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".

Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."

He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber.

"And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.

Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations.

"We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said.

"Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."

Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business.

"I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader said.

"That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."

Predicting that Burnham would call an early general election in spring 2027, Farage attempted to use his speech to convince the public Reform was ready to govern.

Stressing he now had a team of spokespeople with "frontline experience", he said the party was planning to broaden its expertise.

"There are more big jobs to fill, and I'm looking and working on defence, health, and the other areas," he added.

In his speech, Farage also hailed a "historic agreement" on small boat returns, signed earlier between Reform and France's hard-right National Rally party.

The deal sets out how a Reform government would intercept boats in the English Channel and return them to France using the Navy, with France "ordinarily" accepting those on board.

It was signed by the National Rally President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of French presidential elections in April next year, after he gave a speech to the main conference hall.

Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".

He took the opportunity to walk through the crowd and greet delegates during the delay.

His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".

They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.

Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".

Reform is no longer consistently topping national opinion polls, after more than a year of enjoying a comfortable lead.

Meanwhile, Labour's ratings have risen since Burnham entered Downing Street, and Reform has lost some support to Restore Britain, the new right-wing party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

News.title: Oasis fans say cryptic codes in chip shop video point to Glasgow gigs next year
News.content:
Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.

The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.

Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.

It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.

It follows the Gallagher brothers' hugely successful reunion tour which saw them perform at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries.

This included three dates at Murrayfield Stadium, Edinburgh, in August 2025, when they played to 200,000 fans.

News.title: Cambridge launches review into support for Jason Arday before death
News.content:
The University of Cambridge has launched an independent review into its "decision-making and actions" in the period leading up to former professor Jason Arday's death.

The review will examine the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.

Arday, 41, was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, the week after resigning from his position as professor of sociology of education amid intense scrutiny over allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims.

Announcing the review on Friday, Vice-Chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said the time since his death had been a "period of profound sadness and reflection for the university".

"We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus, but given the devastating outcome, we are still asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more," she said.

"This review will help us answer that question."

In a post on social media, the University of Cambridge said: "University Council took the necessary steps to launch an independent review into the university's decision-making and actions, with a focus on identifying shortcomings and areas for improvement."

The first part of the review will look at the "support, interventions and protections" available to Arday in the period before his death.

Those findings will be reported within three months, allowing recommendations for "urgent action" to be considered and implemented "without delay".

It will be led by Nazir Afzal, chancellor of the University of Manchester and former chief crown prosecutor for the North West of England.

Afzal said in a statement that "it is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity", adding "we must be willing to ask difficult questions".

The second part of the review will examine the wider circumstances of Arday's time at Cambridge, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, mentoring and support arrangements.

It will also look at the university's response to allegations of research misconduct and the support available to academics facing "extraordinary public and media scrutiny".

An independent external chair will be appointed to lead the second part of the review, with an expert panel "including individuals with lived experience" advising it.

It is expected to conclude within six months of the panel being established.

In a video message, Prentice said: "I am conscious that Professor Arday's death has deeply affected black staff and students, as well as our neurodiverse community.

"There has also been an unacceptable rise in racist, hateful, and abusive attacks on our staff and students in online forums and on social media."

In 2023, the sociologist, then 37, became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.

Arday had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. He said similar scrutiny would find comparable errors in the work of other academics.

The allegations emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said the criticism had gone "far beyond scholarly disagreement".

Resigning from his post in August, he added: "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and those I love."

Following his death, his family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

A vigil held in Trafalgar Square was attended by thousands, according to its organisers.

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage of Arday before his death.

News.title: 'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC
News.content:
Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who were shot dead this week when settlers and soldiers entered a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank.

The killing of Omar al-Naasan and Khalil Abu Alia comes amid near-daily attacks by Jewish settlers in the village of al-Mughayyir, south of Nablus.

"We expect that when our sons walk in the street, they are likely to return to you injured or killed," Mohammed Al-Naasan, Omar's father, told the BBC.

Israel's military says it fired on "instigators of a violent riot" and that the incident is under review.

The United Nations says more than 80 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the territory since the beginning of the year.

News.title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
News.content:
The tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week.

It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer.

President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands.

The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details: the islands â over which the European powers had interchanged control throughout the 17th and 18th centuries â were uninhabited at the time the British reoccupied the land. The Argentine settlement had been forced out two years earlier, not by the British but by the Americans. A warship, the USS Lexington, destroyed a fort established there in December 1831 amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights.

Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so.

"Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands.

News.title: Woman whose XL bully dog killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
A woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

News.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather, minister says
News.content:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El NiÃ±o event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El NiÃ±o that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

News.title: Transgender surgery halted over concerns patients were not properly assessed
News.content:
Gender-affirming surgery was halted because of concerns from an NHS committee over whether patients had been "appropriately assessed".

After meeting Welsh government ministers on Friday the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee (NWJCC) said data showed the rate of surgery referrals made by the Welsh Gender Service was "significantly higher" than in England.

It also said the proportion of Welsh patients progressing from referral for some types of surgery was "significantly lower" than across the border.

The NWJCC is the body which instructed Cardiff and Vale University Health Board to halt new referrals and planned surgeries.

The health board is responsible for the running of the NHS gender identity clinic which provides specialist care and support for adults in Wales.

It confirmed on Tuesday that some patients who had been awaiting gender-affirming surgery were already in hospital for their procedures when they were told of the suspension.

The Welsh Gender Service provides referrals for patients living in Wales, but all NHS surgeries are carried out in England.

Gender-affirming surgery includes both masculinising and feminising procedures. They are not reversible.

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come in mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will account for 6% of UK gas output when at peak production but environmental groups say it will provide only 2% of UK use when imports are included.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and further estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Man who died near Notting Hill Carnival is named
News.content:
A man who died after jumping into a canal while fleeing from police near Notting Hill Carnival has been named.

Karnell Kelly, 25, died in hospital after entering the Grand Union Canal off Kensal Road, west London, while being pursued by police officers.

He had fled on foot after the officers attempted to stop him near Harrow Road as he approached the carnival wearing a face covering at about 15:20 BST on Monday, the Metropolitan Police said.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which is investigating, said it was reviewing body-worn video from officers who had chased Kelly down Hormead Road.

Officers and members of the public entered the canal to pull him from the water and he was rushed to a central London hospital, where he was pronounced dead at about 16:40.

News.title: Gavin and Stacey star Rob Brydon's regret at turning down Dolly Parton interview
News.content:
Gavin and Stacey star Rob Brydon says he "regrets" turning down the chance to interview Dolly Parton after choosing to stay on a family holiday.

Brydon fronted the BBC documentary series Honky Tonk Road Trip, where he travelled across the American South to celebrate 100 years of country music.

In it he visited Dollywood, a theme park created by Parton, where Dolly's relatives had traced the lineage of the Parton and Owens sides to Wales.

He was told he could interview Parton if he returned after filming had ended, but chose to stay on his family holiday in Arizona - an opportunity he now wished he had taken because he never got to meet her before she died.

Parton died peacefully in hospital in Nashville on 25 August following a brief battle with cancer. She was admitted to hospital four days before her death with kidney and autoimmune issues.

"I sort of regret it now," he told Lucy Owen during an interview on BBC Radio Wales.

"I kind of wish that I had gone back because I never met her."

News.title: Planes grounded at Gatwick after aircraft stuck on runway
News.content:
Flights at Gatwick Airport were brought to a standstill for nearly an hour after a plane became stuck on the runway.

A Gatwick spokesperson said the runway was closed for 50 minutes on Friday afternoon because of a "technical issue with a departing vehicle".

The airport said the plane was towed away from the runway, which "reopened shortly afterwards following a full safety inspection".

"As always, safety and security is our number one priority," the spokesperson said.

News.title: Sheep stolen from Clarkson's Diddly Squat Farm
News.content:
Eleven sheep have been stolen from Diddly Squat Farm belonging to presenter Jeremy Clarkson.

Thames Valley Police said it received reports on Wednesday that the animals had been taken from the farm in Chadlington, Oxfordshire, within the last 10 days.

It said officers spoke with Clarkson at the scene on Thursday, adding that no arrests had been made and anyone with information should get in contact.

The 66-year-old told The Sun, external he discovered the animals were missing when he went to count his flock with Clarkson's Farm co-star Kaleb Cooper.

Simon Cowell’s recent back surgery was a “success”, according to his fellow America's Got Talent judge Howie Mandel.

Cowell, 66, has undergone a series of operations in recent years after he broke his back in an electric bike accident in 2020.

Speaking to E! News on Thursday, September 3, 70-year-old Mandel revealed that at that point Cowell was “just hours out of surgery”.

He added: “I heard that it was a success, everything’s okay.”

Kenan Thompson filled in for Cowell on the talent show this week, with Heidi Klum set to take his place next week.

'America's Got Talent' judges Simon Cowell and Howie Mandel together in 2022 ( Vivien Killilea/Getty Images for Cold Stone Creamery )

Mandel joked that he hadn’t yet spoken to Cowell because: “I don't know that, this close to surgery, if this is the first thing you need to see.”

The comedian added that he “can't wait to see him and visit him and give him my best wishes.”

Cowell’s injuries stopped him from appearing in the 2020 season of Britain’s Got Talent. He was temporarily replaced by the show’s previous winner Ashley Banjo.

After he recovered, Cowell said he was “lucky to survive” the ordeal. He told OK! magazine in 2022: “I didn’t talk about it too much at the time. I kept a lot back. It was a lot worse than people thought. I had a lot of long-term nerve damage as well.”

He admitted: “If there was one good thing about lockdown, it was that it gave me the time to heal because I wasn’t working on a TV show. I was able to walk a lot and strengthen my legs.”

In 2022, the TV personality had another e-bike crash that saw him hospitalized with a broken arm, badly bruised cheek and possible concussion. However, the injuries were not as serious as his first accident and he was released from the hospital that same day.

Cowell is known for his brutally honest judging style on reality competitions like AGT, The X Factor and American Idol. He is also hailed as a successful talent scout, having put together massive acts like One Direction and Fifth Harmony.

AGT’s current season 21 marks Cowell’s eleventh season as a judge on the show, although he has been an executive producer since the show’s creation in 2006.

Hosted by Terry Crews, the show usually features Cowell alongside fellow judges Sofía Vergara, Howie Mandel and Mel B.

The final competition and the finale episode will air September 22 and 23.

NFL career rushing leader Emmitt Smith is being sued by a Native American investment company over claims that the former Dallas Cowboys running back and his business partners misappropriated a $2.5 million loan that was supposed to fund a wind farm project in Texas.

Kituwah LLC claimed in a lawsuit filed this week in Delaware that 4 13 Solutions used the money to repay an investor from previous dealings with Smith's company. Kituwah seeks to invest in business opportunities for the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

Kituwah's attorneys said Smith and the Pro Football Hall of Famer's longtime business partner, David Mosley, misrepresented their efforts to secure a U.S. Department of Energy loan that would have triggered repayment to Kituwah.

Kituwah claims the loan has accrued about $600,000 in interest and is asking a jury to determine damages. A message sent to 4 13 Solutions wasn't immediately returned. There was no information on an attorney for Smith or his company in the filing.

According to the lawsuit, Darrel Wilson of Wilson Holdings of North America LLC told Kituwah that he accepted a $2.5 million payment from Smith's company and said he didn't know what triggered the payment. Kituwah's attorneys said it was, “Essentially, like a ponzi scheme.”

Kituwah claims Wilson Holdings was supposed to be repaid only after the wind farm project between Austin and San Antonio, called Project Exodus, secured permanent financing.

“Smith and Mosley knew this was improper,” the lawsuit said. “Instead of telling the truth, they represented to Kituwah that 4 13 Solutions had used the money to acquire Project Exodus as promised, but that the acquisition had been held up for one reason or another.”

The lawsuit claims Smith and his partners never met the requirements for securing government funding and repeatedly made excuses for why the project wasn't proceeding or stopped responding to requests.

Kituwah said it delivered the funds on Sept. 1, 2023, with the expectation of being paid back within months. The lawsuit said 4 13 Solutions promised the wind farm would be operational by December 2024, but Kituwah had seen no evidence the project even existed just a month before that date.

Kituwah said Smith and his partners claimed the wind farm project was valued at $396 million and would generate nearly $14 million in net income in its first year.

The 57-year-old Smith spent the first 13 of his 15 seasons with the Cowboys, won three championships and was the MVP of Super Bowl 28. He broke Walter Payton's rushing record in 2002 and finished with 18,355 yards.

Lawyers for Maria Bartiromo have rejected reports that the anchor has been terminated or has left Fox News Media, calling the claims inaccurate and threatening potential legal action.

Bryan Freedman, an attorney representing Bartiromo, told The Independent that his client remained with the company despite reports surrounding her status.

“For many years, Maria Bartiromo hosted three number-one-rated television shows on Fox channels,” Freedman said.

“She has been, without question, one of the hardest-working journalists throughout her award-winning career. The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false.

“Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise. Those reporting her firing or the incredulous facts supporting that fiction have exhibited a complete and utter reckless disregard for the truth.”

open image in gallery An attorney for Maria Bartiromo pushed back on reports that she was fired or left Fox News Media, dismissing the claims as false and raising the prospect of legal action ( AFP/Getty )

Freedman, a high-profile media lawyer who previously handled high-stakes separations for figures including Megyn Kelly, Chris Cuomo, Tucker Carlson and Don Lemon, issued the statement following widespread coverage of Bartiromo’s abrupt absence from the network.

The dispute follows a brief announcement from Fox News Media stating that the network was parting ways with the long-time presenter after 12 and a half years, thanking her for her work, and wishing her the best in future endeavors.

Reporting by media watchdog Status subsequently alleged that Bartiromo was let go after sharing an internal company guidance with the Trump administration. The internal directive reportedly instructed network personnel to avoid amplifying unsubstantiated election claims made by Donald Trump during a speech.

Reports also indicated that Bartiromo’s top producer, Patrick Ignozzi, was no longer with the network.

The sudden shift led to swift reactions across political and media circles. Trump defended the host on Truth Social, calling her a “total professional” and a “true warrior.” Eric Trump praised her as “the hardest-working person in media” in a post on X, calling the departure a major loss for the network.

open image in gallery Donald Trump praised his long-time ally as a ‘true warrior’ while rumors circulated that she could be considered for a White House role ( Reuters )

Fox has already moved to adjust its program lineup. Mornings with Maria on Fox Business is being rebranded as Mornings with Fox Business with rotating anchors. Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street has been renamed Fox Business Network’s Wall Street, hosted this week by Cheryl Casone, and Jason Chaffetz was tapped to host Sunday Morning Futures.

Speculation briefly linked Bartiromo to a potential role within the White House following the departure of former press secretary Karoline Leavitt. However, reporting from Vanity Fair indicated she was not pursuing a position in the administration.

Throughout her tenure, Bartiromo remained a prominent conservative media voice and frequent interviewer of Trump. During an April broadcast, Trump told her he was “very surprised” crude oil prices were at $92 a barrel, adding, “it’s going to come dropping down very big as soon as it's over.”

In another notable broadcast, Bartiromo mistakenly cited a parody post as authentic, telling former Representative Dan Crenshaw, “I love the way the president handled it because, congressman, he put out a tweet... The president had fun with that!”
