Jingili-Mudburra native title holders hope the Beetaloo brings jobs and royalties for their people.

Native title holder Rosemary Raymond described her remote home of Elliott as a "forgotten town".

"There's nothing there, there's no future," she said.

Rosemary Raymond, left, says gas from the Beetaloo can provide a better future for her people. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

She was asked at a press conference at the Beetaloo what she thought about the calls from green groups based in Sydney and Melbourne for the Beetaloo project to be shut down.

"Nup — it's our land, it's our statement to say, we need a better future for our children," she said.

"Don't care what the Greens say; it's our decision, and this is our land."

Backers of the Beetaloo Sub-Basin project say it will bring huge economic benefits to the Northern Territory. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The Beetaloo's long-standing critics would argue that it is still largely undetermined how much in benefits will go to the native title holders from the Beetaloo during the project's lifespan.

It's an argument not likely to be settled quickly.

Now that Beetaloo gas has begun to flow, on one side of the fence there's elation, and on the other, bitter disappointment and frustration.

The start of fracking in the NT has shown that some fractures in Australian society remain as deep as ever.

World.title: George Russell hits back for Mercedes in Monza practice
World.content:
Formula 1 title contender George Russell has hit back at early pacesetters Ferrari with the fastest lap of ​the day for Mercedes in Italian Grand Prix practice.

Russell surged to the top of the standings in second practice at the fast Monza circuit.

His lap ​of one minute and 22.559 seconds was ‌0.120 quicker than Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who was second in session two.

Russell served a notice of intent ahead of Sunday's race, which he needs to win to close the 59-point gap to championship-leading teammate Kimi Antonelli.

Leclerc had clocked a best time of 1:23.008, which was 0.173 quicker than Ferrari teammate Lewis Hamilton, in the first practice session.

"There's still some work ahead of us as our competitors look strong, but ⁠so far the feeling with the car was solid," Leclerc said.

Seven-time champion Hamilton was fifth in the second session.

Antonelli, who is set to start from the back of the grid due to engine penalties, was third fastest in the second session and 0.141 off the pace.

McLaren's reigning world champion, Lando Norris, was fourth, while his Australian teammate, Oscar Piastri, was sixth in the second session.

Norris has won the past two races and will be chasing a hat-trick on Sunday.

"The pace isn't where we need it to be right now," Norris said.

Gasly docked Monaco podium

Alpine's Pierre Gasly was stripped of his third place at the Monaco Grand Prix and Isack Hadjar reinstated to third position following a successful appeal by two Formula 1 teams.

Gasly dropped to seventh place in the June 7 race after ​a pair of ‌five-second penalties were applied.

Pierre Gasly was relegated to seventh place in the Monaco Grand Prix standings. (Getty Images/NurPhoto: Luca Rossini)

Initially, the penalties for speeding infractions had been rescinded one week after the race.

McLaren and Red Bull appealed to ‌the FIA's International Court of Appeal, with a hearing held ⁠in Paris on August 25.

The decision to ‌reinstate the original finish order ​was announced Friday.

Piastri was elevated to fourth place following the successful appeal.

Reuters

World.title: Triple-murderer Darryl Young previously jailed for cattle theft
World.content:
This is where convicted murderer Darryl Valroy Young shot dead his three new neighbours and almost killed another on an August morning in 2022.

The entrance to Shannonvale Station, at Bogie in north Queensland, is at the end of a corrugated dirt road through eucalypt and hardwood timber forest.

Passing over cattle grids and through a steep dip into a creek bed, there's a climb up a hill to the property entrance.

Three padlocks on a thick chain keep unwanted visitors out and a large "no trespassing" sign warns that admittance is by invitation only.

The text on the "legal notice" sign is a template from the sovereign citizen movement proclaiming an "exclusion notice" applies to council officers, police, sheriffs and bailiffs with a minimum financial penalty of $10,000.

A fading yellow "smile you're on camera" sign is to the right of two trail cameras strapped to the fence; a reminder that you are being watched.

Trail cameras are tied to the gate at Shannonvale Station. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

It was here, in front of the gates, where the bodies of Mervyn, 71, and Maree Schwarz, 59, and her 35-year-old son, Graham Tighe, were found.

They had been shot in the head with a .30-30 calibre rifle. The casings were found in the dirt.

Graham's brother, Ross Tighe, was also shot, but escaped and raised the alarm.

An 'angry' call

Darryl Young was found guilty in the Supreme Court in Townsville on Friday of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder.

During the course of the trial, the jury heard Young's anger towards his neighbours escalated over missing cattle.

A phone call Graham Tighe received over a knock-off beer was recounted to the court by his best mate and cattle contract musterer Shane Dendle.

Graham Tighe was shot dead at a cattle property at Bogie in north Queensland on August 4, 2022. (Facebook)

Shannonvale Rd leads to the Young property. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

He heard Young use a loudspeaker to accuse the neighbours of stealing his calves as he had found some of his cows with full udders of milk but no calves.

"He was angry," Mr Dendle said of Young's tone.

"[Graham] said he's not pinching the calves, he has got enough on."

Then partner of Ross Tighe, Caitlin Jordan, said Young then demanded they meet.

"Darryl said, 'I'm sick of all this'," she recalled.

"He said, 'No you will meet me at the border of Shannonvale at the front'. Graham said, 'What time?' Darryl said, '8am and it will be you, your brother, Merv and Maree, you will all be present'."

"He reiterated that about three times."

Old cars here and there punctuate property turn offs. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

The gate meeting

The crime scene is near the boundary of the Schwarz's and Tighe's Sutherland Station and Young's Shannonvale Station, which was a 20-minute drive for the victims.

Ross Tighe said the family — amid a cattle muster — set off the following morning in two vehicles headed for Young's Shannonvale Station gate.

Riding with his brother, Ross Tighe said he fixed the clock in the LandCruiser ute and they arrived at the gate just before 8am on August 4, 2022, to find Young, already sitting in his Nissan Navara waiting, inside his property.

Ross Tighe said Young told Graham to hang a Shannonvale Station key on the gate — which he did before he and his brother sat in silence for 10 minutes awaiting their mother and stepfather.

Maree (left) and Mervyn Schwarz (middle), and Graham Tighe were found dead outside the gate of the Bogie cattle station. (Supplied/ABC News)

When they arrived, Mervyn Schwarz approached Young for a handshake.

"Darryl said, 'I won't shake your f**king hand'," Ross Tighe said.

"He said that he saw cows of his with full udders of milk — implying that we were pinching his calves. He said it made him feel sick.

"He said he would give us two weeks to give them back or he would do something about it."

Darryl Valroy Young pleaded not guilty to all charges during the trial. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Family gunned down

Ross Tighe said the family denied the accusation then Young walked to the back driver's side door of his Navara.

"He didn't say anything he just walked to his car, just casually, and pulled out a gun," Mr Tighe said.

"He said, 'I'll end this once and for all.'

"He shot Merv in the face, and I turned around to start running."

He said he ran to take cover behind the family's two parked vehicles but was shot in the stomach before he reached them.

"I saw Graham had been shot as well, he was on the ground, we made eye contact and he was making a noise like he was in pain," he said.

"I could see [Mum] from under the car, she had been shot, she was on her knees and holding her stomach area."

Ross Tighe said he ran, covered himself in long grass and hid for about 10 minutes.

He said during that time he heard two more gunshots before he made his way back up the slope he had run down while hiding behind trees.

A washed-out creek crossing survivor Ross Tighe had to get over. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

He said Young and his Navara were gone and he could see his mother and Graham Tighe had both suffered gunshots to the head.

"I was telling myself on the way back they are all going to be dead. I didn't look for Mum, and then I opened the car door because it was already running, and I saw her in there," Ross Tighe said.

"She was f**king shot in the head — through the window."

Call for help

He said he took the family's other car from the gate and drove about 7 kilometres, puncturing a tyre in the process, towards Sutherland Station and saw Shane Dendle driving a truck.

Mr Dendle described the moment to the trial through tears.

"I met Rosco on the road, he was in the old Toyota, he was coming in pretty hot," he said.

"You could tell he was hurt, he was holding his guts."

Mr Dendle and Ms Jordan called emergency services and eventually Ross Tighe was transported via helicopter to Mackay Base Hospital where surgeons ultimately decided not to remove a projectile from his hip bone.

A 'miracle' survivor was found

What the jury did not hear was that Darryl Young and his mother had been convicted and sentenced for stealing cattle from neighbouring properties and selling them in 2003.

It is almost impossible to get anyone to talk about the long-running conflict over fences and allegations of cattle theft that led to the murders.

People say they have to live in the community and interact with other members and connections of the Young family.

Former Bowen mayor Mike Brunker. ( ABC News: ABC North Qld: Lily Nothling )

One who will talk is former Bowen mayor Mike Brunker, who says it's a miracle Ross Tighe was found alive.

Mr Brunker said if Mr Tighe had not survived, justice might never have prevailed.

He said Young, now 63, was frequently in conflict with previous neighbours before the Schwarz family bought Sutherland Station a year prior to the attack on their family.

"The big joke was when he [Darryl Young] said he got on well with his neighbours … that was a fabrication," Mr Brunker said.

He said the previous owner of Sutherland Station sold it due to "constant heartache and battles with the Youngs".

"Everyone in town knew what sort of person he was. The jury's decision won't be a surprise," he said.

"They know what has been done in the past, what he's like."

Remote community

Bogie is home to just over 200 people who live on large cattle properties, according to the 2021 Census.

It is roughly 32 kilometres from the small mining town of Collinsville and about 55km south-west of coastal Bowen.

After passing paddocks of green tomato plants on the Bowen Development Road, a dirt turn-off marks the start of the two-and-a-half-hour drive to the Young's property.

The turn-off to Bogie from the Bowen Developmental Rd. (ABC Tropcial North: Danielle Jesser)

It is hard to get above 60km/h on Normanby Road once you leave the bitumen.

At first, the country is fenced with star pickets and barbed wire, which eventually gives way to unfenced properties where fat cattle graze on either side of the road.

Bogie is prime cattle breeding country. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Red-tailed black cockatoos take flight and wallabies bounce off as vehicles approach.

Bush orchids are high in the trees and the white trunks of gums contrast with the dark hardwood trees.

Large granite boulders, grass trees and a trickle of water is all that is left in some creeks after summer rain.

In the wet season, the three crossings of the Bogie River and other seasonal creeks run a banker; a displaced concrete culvert is evidence of the torrent that can arise.

The first of three Bogie River crossings. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Such is the remoteness of these parts, Mr Brunker is thankful Ross Tighe survived to tell the tale.

"Had he not, they might never have found their bodies. It's a very remote part of the country, it's rough and there are mining shafts," he said.

"For what he's gone through and for the defence to say he did it to put doubt in the jury's mind … he should rot in hell."

Mr Brunker said Mr Tighe should hold his head high after not only being shot, but having to relive the experience in court.

"To be shot in the guts and thinking he [Young] would come after him, it was superhuman what he did."

A sentencing hearing will be held for Darryl Young in Townsville on Monday.

World.title: Before David Hockney painted the pool, he faked his art college diploma
World.content:
It was an expired driver's licence that spurred on one of the 20th century's most prolific art series.

British-born Los Angeles native David Hockney was stuck in New York with said expired licence when he began experimenting with colours, collage and transparent mylar sheets at lauded printmaker Kenneth Tyler's home, where he stayed for 49 days.

Delving into its own collection, the National Gallery of Australia (NGA) has unearthed a wealth of the artist's earlier works, pre-fame, from his days at the Royal College of Art to his first summer in Los Angeles, where he picked up the knack for the aforementioned signature style.

Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures), painted by David Hockney (not featured in the NGA exhibition) sold for more than $124 million at auction in 2018. (Supplied: Christie's/David Hockney)

The exhibition underscores Hockney's pivotal collaboration with master printmaker Tyler.

The NGA holds more than 1,000 Hockney works, in what it describes as one of the most significant collections of Hockney in the Southern Hemisphere.

One of the NGA's most sought-after Hockney works, a Bigger Grand Canyon, is currently on loan to the Louis Vuitton Museum in Paris.

There are intimate portraits of past lovers, family, and friends from the 1960s, 70s and into the 1980s, showing some of his first colour prints and crayon drawings.

The exhibition features traditional mediums like etching, lithography, and photography alongside experimental tools such as the mylar sheets he used to create some of his famed pool pieces, and fax machines, tracing how portraiture anchored Hockney's work.

The show also features a set of iPad self-portraits, Hockney still exploring different art mediums even in to his 80s.

Head curator of international art at the National Gallery of Australia, Magda Keaney, in front of David Hockney's An image of Gregory, 1984-85. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"I think really what that shows is that unfathomable creative drive and sense of experimentation in his art," NGA head curator of international art, Magda Keaney, says.

"So he's working across different media, but when he's working in portraiture you can come back to some central things, you come back to the face, you come back to that sense of intimacy, you come back to relationships."

Hockney took inspiration from the faces he saw around him, particularly in early works depicting British fashion designer and close friend Celia Birtwell, who was an early muse for the artist.

There are works spanning decades, intimately graphing their relationship.

Hockney's Red Celia, 1984. (Supplied: NGA)

Hockney eventually also began taking inspiration from those who came before him, as the displayed works follow him into the 1980s, when he "started exploring portraiture through other aesthetic means such as cubism and really interrogating how we see perspectives in pictures that comes from his great love of the artist Picasso", Ms Keaney says.

Celia received the Picasso treatment herself, in one of the larger, more colourful pieces in the exhibition that almost acts as an anchor to Hockney's other works in the exhibition.

Another work of Hockney's of his friend and fashion designer, Celia. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A Rake's Progress

Described by King Charles as one of life's true originals: "One who wore his genius as lightly as those beloved yellow Crocs of his that helped brighten Palace occasions", even his earlier works were full of signature Hockney, who, just quietly, refused to paint Queen Elizabeth.

One piece that exudes his signature mischief is Hockney's A Rake's Progress, a semi-autobiographical series of 16 etchings and aquatints created between 1961 and 1963, re-imagining William Hogarth's famous 18th-century moral narrative series of the same name.

Also on display, the famed artist's faked art school diploma, which he submitted in place of his final course assignment at the Royal College of Art.

Early works of Hockney's, such as We Two Boys Together Clinging and Two Men in a Shower, celebrated gay relationships when homosexuality was still illegal in Britain, and while those are not featured in this exhibition, his experiences are tracked through sketches as a gay man finding his identity in his early career.

Hockney's A Rake's Progress, a semi-autobiographical series of 16 etchings. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"Hockney's identity and his relationships are really integral to his work, and that's something he explores with some of his earliest works in the show," Ms Keaney says.

"The Rake's Progress, a group of prints where he humorously reprises Hogarth's parable [sic], but it's about Hockney's first trip to New York as an art school student, and that's a group of work in which he shows and depicts his identity as a gay man.

"His excitement coming from Bradford in the North of England, being in New York, discovering gay bars and being able to watch TV to 3am."

Director of the National Gallery of Australia, Dr Nick Mitzevich, in front of David Hockney's An image of Celia, 1984-86. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"It's very important to put the collection to work, and this exhibition displays that continuing strategy in celebrating the collection we have assembled from the early 70s into the present day," NGA director Nick Mitzevich says.

" It's a rich collection to mine. "

Dr Mitzevich says in the future, the gallery looks forward to giving the Australian public more of Hockney.

"We will be making announcements about further engagement with the collection, our immense holdings of David Hockney," he says.

"As a gallery director, you have to keep things up your sleeve."

World.title: Construction sector probe likely to put Mick Gatto back in the spotlight
World.content:
Mick Gatto isn't worried about the upcoming royal commission into Victoria's building industry.

"A royal commission don't bother me," he confidently declared on Karl Stefanovic's podcast in late July, days before Ben Carroll announced the inquiry in his first move as Victoria's new premier.

"They'll spend another $100 million, it'll be a witch hunt … and they'll come up with nothing, like they have in the past," Mr Gatto casually predicted.

The upcoming royal commission will investigate serious allegations of wrongdoing on major public building sites.

They include accusations that bikies and organised crime figures infiltrated both the once-powerful construction union, the CFMEU, and building companies working on taxpayer-funded infrastructure projects under the Victorian government's Big Build.

The cost to taxpayers of all this alleged corruption has been reported at $15 billion, a figure disputed by the former premier Jacinta Allan.

Barrister Geoffrey Watson SC is the man behind that whopping estimate.

He investigated the industry for the CFMEU's administrator and wrote a report that also put Mr Gatto firmly in the spotlight.

In his report, Mr Watson said that Mr Gatto, who runs a mediation business in the construction industry, had previously been referred to during civil proceedings as a "standover man" and by the National Crime Authority as "the head of a criminal network" — allegations Mr Gatto has previously denied.

Mr Watson reported Mr Gatto had so much influence over the CFMEU in Victoria that he had the power to shut down building sites.

"Everybody knows what he has been doing," the barrister wrote, in his report tabled at a Queensland inquiry into the CFMEU.

"Yet he seems to survive."

An unfair target with a colourful past, Mr Gatto claims

However, he is again facing scrutiny.

In June, Mr Gatto and his wife were arrested at their Mount Martha home was searched by police investigating the building industry.

They seized computers and phones, and the couple was released without charge, with Gatto later characterising the raid as an information-gathering exercise that came up with zero.

This is the sort of pressure most people would find seriously stressful to face publicly.

But Mr Gatto, a former heavyweight boxer, appeared unfazed on a video recording of the former Today host's podcast.

Mick Gatto speaking on Karl Stefanovic's podcast earlier this year. (Youtube: The Karl Stefanovic Show)

Wearing a long gold chain and a black knitted jumper, the 71-year-old's voice was steady as he dismissed Mr Watson's investigation.

"Ninety-five per cent of that report, you can rip it up and throw it in the bin," he said.

"It's completely nonsense and in time, it'll all come out that it is nonsense."

He reckons he has been unfairly targeted because of his colourful past.

That past includes surviving Melbourne's gangland wars in the early 2000s — and being acquitted of a murder charge of his own — when a killing spree broke out in the city's underworld.

Mr Gatto describes himself as someone who was on the periphery of the gangland wars — someone who knew the key players but wasn't one himself.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Jessica Longbottom at jessicalongbottom@protonmail.com. If you're sharing sensitive information, read our tips on how to contact us confidentially.

He rose to national prominence when he was portrayed as a character in the hugely popular Underbelly TV series.

His wife Cheryl Gatto told a defamation trial against the ABC in 2020 that her husband had become so famous that he was routinely asked for selfies when they were out dining.

"I've mentioned to him a couple of times, 'I think you're more recognisable than the Prime Minister," she said in Victoria's Supreme Court.

Mr Gatto declined an interview request from the ABC and did not respond to written questions.

But he told Mr Stefanovic he knows that a high profile comes with scrutiny.

"Honestly mate, I don't do the wrong thing," he declared.

"I've been under the microscope all my life. I know that I'm looked at all the time.

"My phone is bugged. I know all that."

It's widely expected that this upcoming royal commission will probe, amongst other things, whether Mr Watson's allegations about Mr Gatto's work in the construction sector — or Mr Gatto's denials — are correct.

At this stage, neither man is blinking.

The 'Devil of South Melbourne'

Mick Gatto says he became a thief at a very young age.

In his book I, Mick Gatto, he explained that Turkish and Greek clubs near his childhood home in Cecil Street, South Melbourne, had pinball machines rigged for illegal gambling.

"Once I discovered those machines (I was probably six or seven) I was hooked," Mr Gatto remembered.

"I used to do anything to find money to play them: beg, borrow and steal."

The stealing he described was prolific.

Images of Mick Gatto's early boxing career adorned the walls of his gym when the ABC visited a decade ago. (ABC News)

He stole from his brother, from visitors to his family home and even from the firefighters at the station next door.

"We used to break fire alarms or call from a phone box, and when they responded to the alarm we'd go in and take the money from their mess hall," he recalled.

At school, Mr Gatto also found trouble.

He was expelled twice and left school at 13, but one former classmate told the ABC that while teachers found Mr Gatto a "handful", he was a "friendly" student who wasn't involved in fights.

Others didn't think so highly of him, with Mr Gatto saying old women in his neighbourhood took to calling him "the devil of South Melbourne".

Run-ins with the police were common.

As Mr Gatto grew older, he wrote that he became involved in more serious gambling and burglaries.

A job at a golf club led to seven months in prison from December 1982, with Mr Gatto missing the birth of his daughter.

That time inside, he said, turned him off robberies.

But his love of a punt and involvement in gambling remained.

In Melbourne's illegal gambling dens from the 1970s to early 1990s, Mr Gatto thrived.

Above gyms and restaurants, with code words and gamblers in the know, games were played through to the early hours of the morning, often with huge money on the table.

"Games would open and close, depending on money, police raids and different partnerships," Mr Gatto explained in his autobiography.

" I made millions — and gambled away just as much. "

It was from this era that Mr Gatto said he made a wide network of contacts, including underworld figures who would later be key players in the gangland wars.

Mr Gatto survives a killing spree that shocked Melbourne

Many see the 1998 murder of standover man Alphonse Gangitano — who was also known as The Black Prince of Lygon Street — as the start of the gangland wars.

Over nearly a decade, more than 30 men were killed. Mr Gatto knew many of the victims. And the killers.

He blamed the gangland wars on the paranoia of drug dealers who he said were using too much of their own product.

"The main reason I lived was that I had had nothing whatsoever to do with drugs," Mr Gatto wrote in his autobiography.

Police and journalists at the time named Mr Gatto as a member of the so-called Carlton Crew, whose members included Gangitano, Lewis Moran and sons Jason and Mark, as well as Mario Condello and Graham Kinniburgh.

All but Mr Gatto would lose their lives.

Mick Gatto attended Des Moran's funeral in 2009. (ABC TV News)

Mr Gatto denied such a group existed.

"This group and the term were invented by a journalist or the police to try to show there were two factions fighting each other, that just wasn't the case," Mr Gatto wrote in 2009.

But he acknowledges he did have friendships and connections with all these men.

Condello — who was charged with conspiracy to murder Carl Williams and was named in court by police as a man with connections to the Italian mafia — was a business partner of Mr Gatto's in an illegal bookmaking operation in the 90s.

Gangitano was a childhood friend who Mr Gatto said he partied with as a young man.

"Towards the end Alphonse was went off the rails a bit — he was just mad," Mr Gatto remembered.

Kinniburgh and Lewis Moran, he said, he'd known since his teenage years — he was so close to Kinniburgh he called him "pa".

Another key player Mr Gatto said he met through illegal gambling was Carl Williams.

Carl Williams was a high-profile figure in Melbourne's gangland wars. (AAP: Julian Smith)

"He used to come in, have a couple of bets, do his money and we'd give him a cab fare to get home," Mr Gatto recalled.

Williams became a major drug dealer who was eventually convicted of four murders before he was bashed to death inside Barwon Prison in 2010.

Mr Gatto was also friends with the hitman Andrew Veniamin, an ally of Williams, before the pair had a dispute and Mr Gatto shot Veniamin dead in 2004.

He was charged with murder but gave evidence in his trial that Veniamin was shot in self-defence when they wrestled over a gun that Veniamin produced.

Mr Gatto was acquitted.

He revealed after the trial that the jury had not been told he had a body bag in his car at the time of the shooting, along with some bullets.

Mick Gatto leaves the Supreme Court in 2005. (Glenn Hunt: AAP)

"I realise not every bloke has a body bag in his boot, but it was no big deal to me," he wrote in his book.

He said Condello was involved in a funeral parlour and gave him the bag on a whim and it sat in his boot for months.

He said the bullets had fallen out of a friend's gun many weeks before.

These details, he said, had been ruled inadmissible in his trial "for some reason".

Mr Gatto has been asked about his connections to gangland figures in the years since.

He was questioned about his friendship with Veniamin during the defamation case he lost against the ABC, telling the court he had all sorts of friends.

"It is always handy to know people around Australia, which I do," he said.

Mediation work labelled an extortion model

It's this history that likely weighs on people in the construction industry when they receive a call from Mick Gatto.

"Oh, look, there's no doubt about that, you know, the reputation helps. Of course it does," he told the ABC's 7.30 program in 2014 when discussing his mediation work.

However, he insisted he didn't use threats.

" I don't believe in standing over anyone. I don't believe in being aggressive with anyone. "

It was a position he reiterated in an interview with Jaqui Felgate on 3AW earlier this year.

Most of his work, he said, was sorting out disputes between construction companies and the militant CFMEU, ranging from issues on sites to superannuation not being paid.

"A lot of builders are intimidated by the unions," Mr Gatto told Felgate.

"They pay me a retainer. Any union issues they refer it to me, they don't lose productivity, their jobs don't stop."

One construction business owner who was paying Mr Gatto and spoke to the ABC anonymously in order to be frank, said Mr Gatto was a pure professional when he mediated several disputes his company had with the CFMEU.

"He's genuinely done a lot of work and he does it through his contacts in the industry," they said.

But Mr Watson disagrees.

In one phone call referenced in his report and aired by Channel Nine, Mr Gatto was heard telling a developer, "We can cause you grief".

"I know you've got enough grief in your life already," Mr Gatto went on to say.

Mr Gatto later said he called the developer on behalf of a builder because subcontractors weren't being paid, and it wasn't a threat.

CFMEU investigator Geoffrey Watson alleges along with threats, Mr Gatto has been colluding with the CFMEU to create disputes and "extort" builders.

Geoffrey Watson is a barrister who reported on the CFMEU. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The "Gatto extortion model", Watson wrote, involved "demanding money from contractors under the threat that, unless a payment was made, the CFMEU would raise an industrial issue and close a building site".

Given closing a site could cost builders up to $1 million a day or send them into bankruptcy, they often paid up.

In recent years, Mr Watson estimates Mr Gatto has been making at least $5 million a year from more than a dozen builders on his books.

Some of the builders on Mr Gatto's payroll include those who've done work on Big Build projects.

It's likely the upcoming royal commission will probe whether taxpayer money has been flowing to Mr Gatto as a result.

The close relationships the royal commission is expected to probe

Mick Gatto has always said relationships are at the heart of his mediation business.

One source told the ABC they would go to see Mr Gatto at the restaurant Villa Romana on Lygon Street, where Mr Gatto was known to hold court.

People would stop to take photos with Mr Gatto, they said, and one time they remembered Mr Gatto pulling crisp $50 notes out of his wallet and giving hundreds of dollars to a man who was down on his luck.

"He was always at a table for 18. It would be filled with rotating people — bikies, union figures, former cops," they said.

"When Mick makes an ally, they stick with him."

And Mr Gatto had plenty of allies in the CFMEU.

Mr Gatto's seeming leverage with the union has been built over almost half his life.

In 1995 he was phoned by a young union official by the name of John Setka who was leading a strike outside a North Melbourne factory, he recalled in his biography.

Mr Setka called because he and the workers felt threatened by a notorious ex-copper hired by the company.

The former copper was someone Mr Gatto knew from his childhood run-ins with police.

That connection helped Mr Gatto broker a deal.

It was his first ever intervention in an industrial dispute and mediation work after that just snowballed, he said in his book.

It was the start of an enduring friendship with Mr Setka.

John Setka stood down as the secretary of the CFMEU's Victorian branch in 2024. (AAP: Joe Castro)

Mr Setka, who'd already made a name for himself by causing trouble on building sites, went on to head the CFMEU in Victoria, and his relationship with Mr Gatto would endure for decades.

Mr Setka stood down as head of the CFMEU when allegations first surfaced of union corruption in 2024.

Labelled "abusive" and "corrupt" by Geoffrey Watson in his report, Mr Setka has been found in breach of several industrial laws over his long career and in 2019 was found guilty of harassing his then-wife.

He's currently facing several charges over allegations he made online threats to people including the union's former administrator.

"I love John," Mr Gatto told Mr Stefanovic on his podcast.

"He is a union leader, mate, through and through. He only knows attack. If someone challenges him, he attacks."

Corruption-busting barrister questions whether money made it to union

Mr Watson alleges Mr Gatto's relationship with the CFMEU has made him tens of millions of dollars over the years, and in some cases it's unlikely that CFMEU officials went unrewarded.

Mr Gatto has always maintained he never paid the union anything for their cooperation.

The union was placed in administration in 2024. (ABC News)

His relationships at the CFMEU became a 'badge of honour' among some members of the union hierarchy, one industry source said.

Mr Gatto even bought some members of the team gold Versace bracelets, which were presented to them in small velvet bags, according to Watson's report.

Mr Watson described it as a symbol of Mr Gatto's ownership of the CFMEU staffers.

Those who Mr Gatto considers friends have also allegedly benefited from the close relationship.

When underworld figure Faruk Orman was released from jail in 2019 after he had his conviction for murder quashed, he set up some construction companies.

Mr Watson alleges Mr Gatto was able to get the businesses highly desirable workplace agreements with the CFMEU, which granted access to union worksites.

One of the agreements, Mr Watson claims in his report, was on-sold a few days later to another company for $250,000.

Inquiry likely to put Mick Gatto back in the spotlight

While Mr Gatto shrugs off the scrutiny surrounding him, he is obviously paying close attention.

In his recent media appearances he's referenced the more than 200 news articles Nick McKenzie from Nine Newspapers has written about corruption in the building industry, dismissing them broadly as "nonsense."

But there is evidence that even before the royal commission hears from a single witness, his influence is waning.

Mick Gatto at a boxing event at Margaret Court Arena in November 2019. (AAP file photo: Michael Dodge)

The ABC has been told Big Build projects are severing ties with construction businesses that have been known to pay Mr Gatto, and as a result many have taken him off the payroll.

The new CFMEU, under external administration, has issued an edict that no representatives are to contact him.

Mr Gatto admitted as much was true earlier this year, saying he was looking to now deal with builders who didn't have employees with the CFMEU.

What the royal commission has in store for Mr Gatto remains to be seen.

He's already survived two Royal Commissions examining the building industry and union corruption, with no findings against him being made.

But Mr Watson is adamant.

"Now is the time for change. Now is the time finally to break Mr Gatto's malignant influence over the CFMEU and the Victorian building industry," he said in his report.

"Now is the time to get rid of Mr Gatto once and for all."

If 71-year-old Mr Gatto is to be believed, he's already checked himself out.

"I've sort of semi-retired now. I'm just down the beach, do my own little thing, walk the dog," he told Mr Stefanovic.

"I hate coming to the city, to be honest. I've got to put up with all this nonsense."

World.title: Global penguin experts gather at Phillip Island under shadow of climate change, bird flu
World.content:
The world's leading penguin researchers have issued a stark warning about the effects climate change will have on penguin habitats.

The scientists met this week at the 12th International Penguin Conference on Phillip Island, in Victoria's south-east, to discuss the latest research about the seabirds and bird flu management strategies.

At the end of the week-long conference, the researchers released a statement calling for "decisive conservation action" to protect penguins and their habitats.

"When penguins struggle we should pay attention. Their warning is about the health of our oceans and ultimately the health of our planet," the statement said.

" Penguins cannot tell us in words that their world is changing. They are showing us. "

Scientists at the conference discussed the latest penguin research and conservation strategies. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

The call to action comes as the United Nations warns the world will breach the 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming benchmark within the next five years.

Penguins under pressure

Phillip Island Nature Parks senior scientist and chair of the conference Andre Chiaradia said penguins were facing a growing combination of pressures.

He said penguins depend on healthy oceans to survive, and changing oceans could affect where penguins feed, when they breed, how they raise their chicks and whether their populations grow or decline.

He said a major concern for penguins was ice shelves melting at a "scary, fast pace".

Andre Chiaradia says there are many challenges facing penguins globally, including climate change. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

"Those places are disappearing, then there's no place for them to breed," he said.

"Penguins are suffering from a thousand cuts so [bird flu] is just an extra cut on penguins' lives.

"If we do what we can … then we can probably provide a brighter future for penguins."

He said sustainable fisheries, protecting critical feeding and breeding habitats, effective predator management and long-term monitoring could help strengthen the resilience of penguin populations.

Timely event

Phillip Island is home to about 40,000 little penguins, making it the world's largest colony.

This year's conference followed the death in August of a little penguin on the island from H5 bird flu.

So far more than 1,500 penguins have been vaccinated against the disease as part of the government's plan to vaccinate 5,000 of the birds at Phillip Island and St Kilda.

Federation University biological sciences lecturer and speaker at the conference Meagan Dewar said this year's conference was timely.

"It's very important to have so many penguin experts here in the one place as Australia is facing H5N1 outbreaks," she said.

"We have many experts from places that have already experienced this, such as South America and South Africa, and also the Antarctic.

" It's a great time to share knowledge. "

Meagan Dewar says it is very important for penguin experts to gather and discuss research methods. (Supplied: Federation University)

Ms Dewar said Australian experts could learn from other countries' experience of monitoring the disease and how they managed outbreaks.

New research ideas

The researchers also discussed the latest technology used to understand and protect penguins, including artificial intelligence and drones.

US geospatial scientist and conference speaker Brett Buzzanga said one of the biggest benefits was the multiplicity of perspectives and the different knowledge each group had.

"There's a shared language, the shared language of science, the shared language of penguin conservation that everyone wants to collaborate with each other regardless of national borders," Mr Buzzanga said.

Brett Buzzanga speaking at the International Penguin Conference on Phillip Island. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

Mr Buzzanga works with drones equipped with thermal cameras to detect penguins living underground, providing a better picture of penguin populations and how they change over time.

"As with the rest of the world, AI is a big player in being able to classify different images, being able to recognise different patterns in the data," Mr Buzzanga said.

The colony on Phillip Island has about 40,000 birds. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

He said advances in technology allowed researchers to cover much larger areas than they could by hand.

"A lot of the tech unlocks the potential to expand those regions, expand science, expand conservation," Mr Buzzanga said.

"So sharing that with each other, that's the goal."

World.title: A Super title and 25,000 crowds: How Reds plan to make Queensland a powerhouse
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion A Super title and 25,000 crowds: How Reds plan to make Queensland a powerhouse Paul Cully Rugby columnist September 5, 2026 — 9:15am

September 5, 2026 — 9:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Reds chief executive David Hanham and general manager of high-performance Sam Cordingley are basking in the warmer relationship between Rugby Australia and New Zealand Rugby. Talking to the Herald from their offices in Brisbane, they expressed confidence that RA heavies Phil Waugh and Dan Herbert, and New Zealand counterparts Steve Lancaster and David Kirk have provided the stable platform that rugby needs at Test and Super Rugby level. Reds star Carter Gordon celebrates a try against the Brumbies. Queensland have big ambitions for the future. Getty Images There is a Bledisloe Cup Test coming to Brisbane on Anzac Day, a conviction among Super Rugby executives that 10 teams is the right number and confidence that the competition’s best team, the Hurricanes, would stack up well against any club side in the world. “Some of the best players in the world are playing in Super Rugby,” said Cordingley, who played a key role in the recruitment of new Reds coach Vern Cotter.



“If you put the Hurricanes up against any teams in the north, that would most likely be a really good result ... I don’t think it’s a question of talent [in Super Rugby], it’s a question of consistency.” But those more favourable bigger-picture conditions are only one reason why the Reds are, in cricketing parlance, determined to play on the front foot. The Hurricanes claim the 2026 Super Rugby final in Wellington. Their best is as good as any club side in the world. Getty Images Unlike their Super Rugby peers in Australia and New Zealand, the Reds have recorded a series of operating profits, participation numbers in the state are strong and 12 Reds were named in the Wallabies squad to face Argentina this weekend. As a result, Queensland have unambiguously set their sights high.



“We’ve set a five-year vision for the QRU [Queensland Rugby Union] to build ourselves and build Queensland back to being one of the best rugby provinces in the world,” Hanham said. “And part of that is making sure that we’ve got a winning team and a successful football program. Obviously, you can’t be a strong rugby province without winning on the field. Isaac Henry celebrates after scoring a try against the Waratahs. The Reds know success on the field is the most important thing. Getty Images “Keeping in mind when we talk about a rugby province, that’s the community game and the professional game that we’re responsible for. “In five years, we want to grow the game. We’re about 90,000 players [in Queensland]; we want to get to 100,000.



“We want the Reds to be a consistent top-three team, and in that period of time to be winning a title. We want our crowds at Suncorp to get from averaging 15,000 back up to 25,000. “A big part of that is maintaining financial sustainability as a business, and getting the Ballymore development under way. If someone said, ‘What does the best rugby province look like?’ That’s how we define success.” QRU chief executive David Hanham at the soon-to-be-redeveloped Ballymore. Brendan Hertel/QRU Media There are many layers to a project of such ambition, especially in a complex sporting landscape such as Australian rugby. While the New Zealanders are well into the National Provincial Championship, their domestic rugby competition that runs for 10 rounds before three weeks of play-offs, Australian clubs are about to embark on the four-week Super Rugby AUS.



Cordingley, who played for the Ballymore Tornadoes in the short-lived, eight-team Australian Rugby Championship in 2007, acknowledges that lack of exposure for the next tier of players remains a challenge. “I can only speculate on where we [Australian rugby] may have been if we’d retained that competition [ARC] relative to the New Zealand NPC ... or what the Currie Cup has delivered in South Africa,” he said. “Credit to Rugby Australia in terms of being able to invest in that product [Super Rugby AUS] ... but I still think we’re short of where we need to be.” That has forced the Reds to be creative, in high performance and commercially. After Super Rugby AUS, they will embark on a four-game tour of Japan and Italy, courtesy of their partnerships with Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights and Benetton Rugby in Treviso.



Hanham says the Reds have found a way to make these tours “cost neutral”, and Cordingley has been the driving force behind them as a way to accelerate the development of the Reds’ non-Wallabies. In echoes of former Wallaby Ben Darwin’s theories on cohesion, Cordingley says the tour games are not solely about accumulating playing minutes, but increasing what the Reds call “shared experience matches”. “It’s not just playing games of rugby,” Cordingley said. “We have created these partnership opportunities with Benetton and Panasonic to be able to provide experiences for our players and staff collectively to get to what we target – around 30 shared experiences matches a year to be competing with the French Top 14 clubs and the English Premiership.” The Reds are confident Cotter’s arrival will also be step towards their title ambitions, but they also hold firm views about Super Rugby’s structure. There is near-constant chatter about change or expansion, with Japan often mentioned as a possible entrant.



Hanham, however, urged caution. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Cheat code’: Wilson cleared to play in Shute Shield decider after Wallabies standby call “There is a very strong view – I believe shared by the clubs and unions – that we’ve got the right number of teams,” he said. “How do we improve the quality of the competition, in the sense of not only the onfield product, but how we market and promote it? “We’ve now got an Anzac Bledisloe, which I think is a great tent-pole event, like State of Origin is to NRL. We’ve got Super Round, which was a great success in Christchurch ... I feel like we’ve created a product that’s going to be successful. “My personal view is we don’t want to be messing with the integrity of that. However, there is an avenue to enable other competitions to join the Super Rugby Pacific competition at the appropriate times, where you’re not changing the number of teams every year.



“That’s probably been one of Super Rugby’s challenges – it’s constantly changed, too often, over a long period of time. “So, maintain integrity, keep the competition strong and then an opportunity to bring the Japanese competition in at the appropriate time – that will be down the track at some point, I assume, if all the stars align.”

World.title: ‘A real kick in the teeth’: Dozens of tram stops have been upgraded, but wheelchair users still can’t board
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPublic transport ‘A real kick in the teeth’: Dozens of tram stops have been upgraded, but wheelchair users still can’t board Gemma Grant September 5, 2026 — 9:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of tram stops in Melbourne’s north-west built or altered to accommodate the city’s new extra-long G-class trams have failed to provide long-overdue disabled access improvements. Advocates say that the snub has further contributed to the discriminatory nature of the city’s wider tram network. Victoria is years behind a previously legislated deadline to make all tram stops accessible by 2022. A recently merged stop on the route 59 tram, which doesn’t have a level-access platform. Penny Stephens While there is no automatic penalty for missing this target, it opens up the possibility of legal action being brought forward. More than 30 stops across the route 57 and route 59 trams are involved in the network’s “next generation” tram upgrades. Fifteen of these stops have either been merged and relocated or shifted.



The project started in late 2025 and is necessary to accommodate the city’s new G-class trams. The updated design – which commenced public services on June 30 – is 25 metres, longer than previous models. Related Article City life This famous street tries to be all things to all people – and it’s failing But despite the ongoing substantial upgrade works to facilitate the new kind of tram, there are no accompanying plans to improve accessibility by building more “level-access” platforms. This important design feature involves erecting a raised platform that sits in line with low-floor trams such as the G-class. It allows wheelchair users, elderly travellers, people pushing prams and others with access needs to board. Even if a tram has a low-floor design, it can’t cater to those with access needs at a roadside stop.



Disability advocate Andrew Bretherton said it was extremely difficult for people living with disability to navigate Melbourne’s tram system. “It means we can’t get out and access the community. We’re not seen by the broader public … We’re kind of just left isolated in our own homes,” he said. “It’s going to cost [the government] more in the long run anyway because they’ve been mandated to make all these stops accessible. Why are we paying twice for the same thing? It just seems like a real kick in the teeth.” Disability advocate Andrew Bretherton at a North Melbourne tram stop without a level-access platform. Jason South Five additional level-access stops are in development along route 82 following community feedback during 2023 and 2024. Future works along this route to accommodate the G-class trams are also expected to be announced.



On route 57, two level-access platforms were added last year at Queen Victoria Market and at Union Road in Flemington. Major upgrades to the North Melbourne tram corridor are also being considered by the Department of Transport. But just 24 per cent of stops along the entire route 57 have level-access platforms, while half of the stops on the route 59 provide level access. Across the network, only 29 per cent of tram stops provide level access, according to the latest data from the Victoria Auditor-General in March 2025. A further 12 level-access stops were built across the city during the 2024-25 financial year, slightly more than the original target of eight.



Bretherton called the current state of the network a form of segregation and said the state government had broken its promise. Related Article Public transport Fares aside, Hailey pays a ‘physical cost’ for each trip on Melbourne’s old trams “[The government] thinks it’s in a microcosm, where we can just shed off disability,” he said. “It reinforces that burden narrative that is often forced or placed onto the disability community.” A spokesperson from the Department of Transport did not respond to questions on why level-access platform upgrades had not been scheduled to coincide with the other works on the 57 and 59 routes. They said level platform upgrades were currently in progress at stops in other suburbs – including Footscray, Northcote and Brunswick.



“We are delivering upgraded tram stops for the new larger G-class trams to make it easier and safer for more Victorians to take trams to school and work,” the spokesperson said. Recent changes to route 59 stops associated with the G-class tram works have also prompted a mixed response from Flemington residents. One, Haydn Moyle, said stops in his suburb were moved suddenly, and the short community consultation period coincided with the Christmas holiday. Moyle is particularly critical of the decision to move the stop at the corner of Wellington Street and Mount Alexander Road. The former stop was positioned at an existing signalised pedestrian crossing, which made it easy to walk to the nearby primary and high schools.



The stop has since been merged with its neighbour as part of the upgrades and is now roughly 150 metres down the street. The Department of Transport recently finished building a signalised crossing at the new location. Moonee Valley City Council also built a small pocket park at the former tram stop site, which acted as an informal extension of the waiting area for city bound trams. Mayor Rose Iser said this would remain an important community space. Moyle said: “I realised they were changing the [stop] here, and I thought that was really stupid. Because that’s obviously the best place for the tram, for the convenience of local people.” Haydn Moyle at the site of the former tram stop, where a pocket park was built by the council. Penny Stephens “You’ve got 1500 kids every morning who are traversing the roads. So it’s important to get it right,” he said.



But Peter Egan, who owns bike repair shop Smooth Cycles on Mount Alexander Road, said moving the stop would improve road safety in the area. Egan said the busy Flemington intersection was confusing and dangerous for cars and pedestrians. He said there were road incidents every fortnight and near misses even more frequently. “It’s taking one aspect of complexity out of the intersection,” Egan said. “It’s a good thing … I find it a minor inconvenience for people.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Who should (and shouldn’t) be the next James Bond?
World.content:
All we know for certain is that, whatever decision the producers make, it will be a massive deal. After all, there hasn’t been a new 007 in more than two decades. With the final result shrouded in mystery, members of this masthead’s Culture team round up their top – and most unhinged – guesses about who could become the next Bond.

From Callum Turner to Jacob Elordi, who will be the next 007?

Could it be another suave British gent such as Turner? Or perhaps a more roguish character like Dickinson? Or maybe Amazon MGM, which recently bought the Bond franchise from the Broccoli family, could go in an entirely new direction and pick a woman.

There are six in the running, if Page Six is to be believed – Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Harris Dickinson, Paul Mescal, Jack Barton and Australia’s Jacob Elordi – who have already auditioned for the coveted role.

Denis Villeneuve, director of the upcoming Bond film, has reportedly managed to whittle it down to a few top contenders.

It has been the question on everyone’s mind since Daniel Craig hung up his tux five years ago: who will be the next James Bond?

From Beast and Luther to the Fast & Furious franchise, he’s proved himself a worthy action actor with a penchant for grit. There’s probably no room in the world he couldn’t command, particularly with that deep, gravelly voice of his. And even if he’s not into the idea, a black Bond could help update a franchise, born in the 1950s, otherwise at risk of going stale.

Elba has made it abundantly clear he won’t be the next 007, going so far as to say some audiences simply aren’t ready for a black Bond, and that we shouldn’t “try and make it woke” . But despite his protestations, I still think Elba would be the perfect new superspy.

Who should be the next James Bond? Idris Elba

Just picture it: Turner as Bond and Dua Lipa as Bond girl. Bloody brilliant.

And bonus points if his wife, pop sensation Dua Lipa, cameos as one of the new Bond girls. Surely, everyone would love to see her walk out of the ocean in slow motion.

Ian Fleming surely manifested Callum Turner from beyond the grave. He’s British, tall (but not bizarrely so), effortlessly charming and has impeccable bone structure. His endearing ears then offer the je ne sais quoi – that zest that sets him apart, just as every 007 agent should.

Who will be the next James Bond? Callum Turner

I don’t care how tall Jacob Elordi is, he ain’t my Bond. I enjoy him as an actor (I didn’t even hate “Wuthering Heights”), but 007 cannot be a “pretty boy”.

It may never happen, but I’ll die on this hill: Cate Blanchett would make a great Bond.

Though some believe she would make a fabulous master villain instead, her natural elegance and icy sophistication scream Bond. Her turn as intelligence operative Kathryn Woodhouse in Steven Soderbergh’s Black Bag last year was beyond believable. Just imagine her dressed in an impeccably tailored suit with a martini in hand. Exquisite.

A female 007? Hell yes. An Australian female 007? Sign me up immediately. Blanchett’s piercing, unyielding gaze and her sharp wit would make for a wonderful secret agent. Her intoxicatingly charming voice alone has the licence to kill.

Idris Elba already has looks that could kill. He may as well be given the licence as well.

Who should be the next James Bond? Paapa Essiedu

Jack Lowden has already played a spy. He may as well do it again.

Lowden showed his best failed-spy-makes-good chops in Slow Horses , and his interest in history in the BBC’s War & Peace , which launched him into global fame. He’s a great actor and, particularly for die-hard Ian Fleming fans, fits the bill perfectly. He would also bring a vulnerability not often explored in Bond – before Daniel Craig at least – so that would shake things up nicely.

Who will be the next James Bond? Jack Lowden

His energy is too youthful, “boy band” and quasi-intellectual to be considered a solid superspy. He lacks the suave charm needed to blend into a room while somehow also commanding it. I also see his face and immediately think of Nate from Euphoria – more villain than hero. I like my Bond rugged, not pristine.

Having made her mark as FBI special agent Dana Scully in The X-Files, playing a spy is no stretch; she would just be swapping teams across the ditch and using a British accent. She grew up between the US and Britain, and that gorgeously cultured voice is part of her DNA; the perennial twinkle in her eye would also prove an asset in a stunning reimagining of the role.

Asked recently about the rumours she wishes were true about herself, Gillian Anderson told Elle she would love to take on 007. “I’d still have a gun … and I’d be a great collector of women,” she quipped.

Paapa Essiedu has the CV to back him up as the next Bond.

At 36, Essiedu has played a hip-hopping Hamlet (for the Royal Shakespeare Company), won an Olivier Award (for his role in All My Sons) and will take on Severus Snape in HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter remake. Nailing 007 would be a cinch.

British actor Paapa Essiedu, hands down – he is mesmerising on screen. Best known for on-screen roles in I May Destroy You – about consent, trauma and recovery – and Falling , in which he plays a priest struggling with his vocation and alcoholism, he started his career in theatre.

Who shouldn’t be the next James Bond? Tom Holland

One of few contenders for the iconic role who has shown his hand about being keen, Holland told Variety’s Awards Circuit podcast a few years ago he would be mad for it. “Ultimately, as a young British lad who loves cinema, I’d love to be James Bond. I’m just putting that out there,” the 30-year-old said. “I look pretty good in a suit.”

That’s a hard agree from me, but there are only so many legendary characters to go around – step aside Peter Parker and son of Odysseus, and let someone else take the spotlight in their perfectly tailored threads.

Step aside, Peter Parker. This role isn’t for you. AP Photo/Evan Agostini

Garry Maddox, senior writer

Who will be the next James Bond? Paul Mescal, George MacKay or Harris Dickinson

It would be fascinating if it wasn’t, but it’s likely the new 007 will be a strong actor who is white, in his 30s (so he won’t age out of the role too quickly), speaks English as his first language, and has a certain physicality.

Since he broke through with Incendies in 2010, Denis Villeneuve has cast both stars who command the screen and diverse and interesting actors, so he might well look beyond the obvious candidates for Bond. After all, Daniel Craig was a surprise last time round.

Good-looking and dapper: Paul Mescal could fit the 007 bill. Getty Images for Kering

But the producers will be mindful the new film will have to work around the world. The likely scale probably means playing into what will be expected of the character: Anglo, good-looking, dapper.

Who should be the next James Bond? Jacob Elordi

He’s a terrific actor, as his Oscar nomination for Frankenstein shows. He looks the part, can play action, romance and drama, and will be 30 when they shoot the new Bond film next year.

I have to disagree with Nell’s view that his energy is too youthful and “boy band”. He grew out of that with The Narrow Road To the Deep North.

Jacob Elordi has proven he has serious acting chops. Perhaps next he will flex his superspy skills. Getty Images

Is his height a problem? They can work around it. Can he deliver Bond’s dry asides? George Lazenby – not the world’s greatest actor – did in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, so I’m sure Elordi, who has hosted Saturday Night Live, will be fine.

Who’s your wildcard? Austin Butler

He was an out-of-the-box pick in Elvis. He can act, has got rugged good looks and can do accents. He’d be worth auditioning.

Who shouldn’t be the next James Bond? Anyone who stars in a superhero franchise



I’m guessing the new 007 will need to be available for at least three films and possibly a smaller role in a spin-off TV series (centring on Q could work, or even M) so that Amazon gets the most value from acquiring Bond. That would be a clash for actors locked into multiple Marvel and DC instalments.

Robert Pattinson is a good enough actor, but he’s still Batmanning. And no to Tom Holland now, though he could work post Spider-Man when he is less boyish.

Elizabeth Flux, arts editor, The Age



Who will be the next James Bond? Callum Turner



Yeah, OK, he’s on the favourites list for a reason, but the thing about the favourites list is that it is boring. They’re favourites because we can already see any of them playing James Bond because they fit into the bullet hole of what’s come before. Sigh. Why bother? This is not a potshot at him specifically. It’s just that Turner is the safest bet on a list of safe bets – he’s at the right point in his career (well known but not pigeonholed) and an actor who would do a nice, solid job. It’s just not a very exciting prospect.

Who should be the next James Bond? Rufus Sewell



Rufus Sewell is criminally underrated as an actor and has been languishing in the only-allowed-to-play-villains corner for far too long. He has the range, experience and the charisma to bring us a Bond with a deeper sense of danger, and who – like Daniel Craig – would push the character further, rather than simply being an elevated copy-paste-competent-reprisal.

Rufus Sewell has been playing the villain for far too long. It’s time for him to Bond up. Courtesy of Netflix

Who’s your wildcard? Christopher Chung

Best known for playing computer genius douchebag Roddy Ho in Slow Horses, most recently Chung has been on our screens in the new adaptation of My Brilliant Career. Genuinely, I think he would be a brilliant Bond. He’s convincing in every role he takes on. He can be suave and funny, and while he doesn’t fit the cookie-cutter shape of the Bonds that have come before him, once you start thinking of him as a potential 007, it just all makes sense.

Christopher Chung is funny, suave and just different enough from previous Bonds to be perfect.

Who shouldn’t be the next James Bond? Callum Turner

Or any of the favourites really (OK, maybe Jack Lowden can stay). When something is as iconic and well loved as James Bond, people will come and see it. It also means that there’s an opportunity there to do something different – we already have a bunch of Bond films, so if we’re going to make more, they shouldn’t be more of the same. Bring in a wildcard or a risky choice. Push the character in a different direction. If the same names keep popping up as obvious choices, then they are too obvious.

Louise Rugendyke, TV editor



Who will be the next James Bond? Jack Lowden

No question. He’s Scottish, like Sean Connery, and has the action chops via Slow Horses, in which he plays hopeless spy River Cartwright, and he’ll soon have the heartthrob credentials when he appears as Mr Darcy in Netflix’s upcoming adaptation of Pride and Prejudice.

Who should be the next James Bond? Jack Lowden



I’m not budging on this.

Phoebe Waller-Bridge rocked a bejewelled tuxedo while winning a Golden Globe for Fleabag. AP

Who’s your wildcard? Phoebe Waller-Bridge

Imagine if they had a female Bond. Waller-Bridge co-wrote Daniel Craig’s final outing as 007 in 2021’s No Time to Die, and the ace thriller Killing Eve, so let’s put her in a suit and get on with it.



Who shouldn’t be the next James Bond? Jacob Elordi



I like him as an actor, but he is too tall. He’d make a great villain, and bad guys always get to have more fun.

Debbie Cuthbertson, culture news editor



Who should be Bond? Riz Ahmed



Just for the knowing wink to Ahmed’s brilliant series Bait (in which his alter ego, struggling actor Shah Latif, auditions to replace Daniel Craig in the franchise, sparking fevered speculation about the possibility of a “brown Bond”). He’d be a refreshing change from the other candidates.

In his TV show Bait, Riz Ahmed (right) plays obscure actor Shah Latif, who lands a screen test to become the new James Bond.

Who should be the next James Bond? Jack Lowden

I’m with Kerrie and Louise, for all the reasons they articulate, but mainly just to have another Scot in the role.

Who’s your wild card: Hannah Waddingham



The Ted Lasso star displayed some mad action skills as an assassin in the recent series Ride or Die. As a glamazonian (Jane?) Bond, Waddingham could shake and stir the whole franchise.

Who shouldn’t be the next James Bond? Jacob Elordi



Elordi was so good in The Narrow Road To the Deep North that I’d hate to see him locked into one role for a decade or more.

World.title: ‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka interrupts US Open match over cannabis smell
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open ‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka interrupts US Open match over cannabis smell Janina Nuno Rios September 5, 2026 — 8:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

World No.1 Aryna Sabalenka had an unusual interruption during her US Open third-round match on Friday, stopping play to alert the umpire to a strong smell of cannabis drifting on to Louis Armstrong Stadium court. Sabalenka, who had made a fast start to go 3-0 ahead before securing a straight-sets win against Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova, raised the issue during her second service game, pointing out the smell before play resumed. Cause for complaint: Aryna Sabalenka. Getty Images “Someone is smoking weed,” top seed Sabalenka told umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore as she was serving 30-0 up. “Would you mind to... because it’s so strong.” Sabalenka later told reporters she was not objecting to anyone enjoying themselves, but pleaded for the smoking to be kept away from the court.



“I was like, guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please to not do it around the tennis courts,” a smiling Sabalenka said. “It’s a bit tricky to handle that smell while you’re trying to compete at your best.” Loading The odour of cannabis has become a familiar — if unwelcome — feature at Flushing Meadows, with players complaining about the distraction in the past. While smoking is not permitted inside the grounds, recreational cannabis is legal for adults over 21 in New York and smoke from people in the surrounding Flushing Meadows-Corona Park can drift into the tennis complex and on to the courts. Sabalenka said she had smelled cannabis before during the tournament but never so strongly during a match, with Friday’s wind apparently carrying the odour into the stadium.



“That strong, yeah. Also, because it was a bit windy,” she said. “I don’t know if it was coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium. “I just hope they are a bit more aware of that stuff,” she added, before laughing when the questions returned to the subject. “Come on, guys. I think there is nothing else to say about weed. I’m just asking people not to smoke it next to the tennis court.” Related Article US Open De Minaur dumped from US Open in straight sets as Kyrgios cocaine ban revealed Pegula echoes concerns World No.3 Jessica Pegula, who was playing at the same time next door in Arthur Ashe Stadium, echoed Sabalenka’s remarks.



“It makes it New York that it’s so kind of all over the place and chaotic,” Pegula said. “But I do think that there are things that maybe could be better suited towards helping the match be a tennis match and not letting other factors kind of interfere.” The incident came amid controversy over the growing presence of influencers and content creators and questions over their impact on players and the on-court atmosphere. “As far as like the influencer things... tennis etiquette, it’s something you have to learn as you go to these events,” Pegula said. “The smoking weed, you probably just shouldn’t do that. I feel like that should be a known thing.” Reuters
