World.title: Total fire ban in place for Sydney as city set to reach 33 degrees
World.content:
NationalNSWWeather Total fire ban in place for Sydney as city set to reach 33 degrees Anthony Segaert September 5, 2026 — 7:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A total fire ban is in effect for Sydney on Saturday, with the city set to reach up to 33 degrees just five days into spring. An extreme fire danger has also been recorded for the region stretching from the coast to Mount Victoria, coming days after Sydney experienced its warmest winter in 167 years of records. Sydney is waking up to a hot Saturday. Danielle Smith Sydney is forecast to record 27 degrees at noon on Saturday, stretching to 33 degrees by 1pm. The Bureau of Meteorology’s Robert Urbaniak said the “very dry, very windy” conditions combined with low humidity would increase the risk of fire.



“There will be mean winds of up to 50km an hour, together with wind gusts of up to 70km an hour. Combined with very low relative humidity, around 20 per cent, that will basically drive the fire danger,” he said. “When the humidity goes right down, it dries out the fuel.” Smoke haze blows into Mona Vale from burn offs on Friday. Steven Siewert The temperatures are above average for this time of year, he said. “The average maximum temperatures [for September[ in Penrith are 23.5 degrees, in the east about 22.5 degrees. And by contrast today we’re looking at a maximum of 32 in Penrith and 33 in the city, around 10 degrees warmer than average.



“These wouldn’t be September records but they are unusually high, especially for early in September, and combined with the wind being so strong, it’s relatively out of the ordinary.” Fire bans are issued by authorities when hot, dry and windy weather conditions dramatically increase the risks of fires breaking out. No fires are allowed out in the open. View post on X Electric barbecues can be used and gas barbecues if they are being used by a responsible adult, no combustible material is within two metres, the operator has access to an “immediate and continuous” supply of water, and if they are being operated within 20 metres of a private dwelling or is in a designated picnic area approved by the relevant authority. The fire danger rating is forecast to return to moderate over the coming days.



As more Sydneysiders flock to beaches, the NSW government this week also announced the installation of two shark listening stations in Sydney Harbour and an increase in the hours shark surveillance drones would be flying along the coastline. More to come Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Meningitis Foundation calls for bipartisan support for free adolescent vaccination programme
World.content:
The Meningitis Foundation is calling for bipartisan support for a fully funded vaccination programme for adolescents.

The foundation told the Health Select Committee that, when it came to meningitis, New Zealanders had "no fence at the top of the cliff, and no ambulance at the bottom either".

The foundation said that two vaccines were required for the "best possible protection": one was for meningococcal B strain, and another for the A, C, W, and Y strains.

"For those who are not eligible to receive a funded vaccine, the total cost of vaccination is $450," the foundation said.

"This is a significant barrier for many families. The foundation considers that there is unequal access to meningitis vaccines, which is leading to preventable deaths and disabilities."

The foundation also wanted Community Services Card Holders to have access to the free vaccination programme, aftercare support for survivors, and improved monitoring and notification of meningitis cases.

Pharmac funded a meningococcal B vaccine for children under five. It also funded meningococcal B and ACWY vaccines for people with certain high-risk medical conditions and those aged between 13 and 25 living in some close-living environments.

This included boarding schools, university halls, military barracks, youth justice residences, and prisons.

Close living situations did not include flatting or other group living situations.

Pharmac said it supported a proposal to give universal access to ACWY vaccines to children between the ages of one and four years old, and another proposal for adolescents who were between 14 and 21 years old.

However, Pharmac told the Select Committee that there had not been clinical support for universal access to the meningococcal B vaccine for adolescents and young adults.

In 2023, Pharmac's Immunisation Advisory Committee recommended declining an application to fund that vaccine for 13- to 25-year-olds.

This was partly because the overall benefits of the vaccine were not considered proportionate to its costs and risks.

Pharmac had asked its Immunisation Advisory Committee to reconsider its previous recommendation regarding meningococcal vaccination during its May 2026 meeting.

A spokesperson said the records from that meeting were still being finalised and were expected to be released in September.

The Minister responsible for Pharmac, David Seymour, said it made funding decisions independently of the government.

"Pharmac currently fund two vaccines used to prevent meningitis, and are considering a number of applications to widen access to both Meningococcal vaccines. This includes widening access for this these vaccines to include children and young people currently outside the funding criteria."

Health NZ said it had made significant improvement in childhood immunisations, with 83.5 percent of children fully immunised at two years old in the quarter to March 2026, compared to 79.3 percent in the quarter to March 2025.

It said that since June 2023, it had taken steps to increase awareness among vaccinators and target populations.

World.title: Australian man charged over 'offensive' calls to overseas MPs' offices from NZ
World.content:
An Australian man has been charged by New Zealand and Australian police for allegedly making threatening phone calls to electorate offices while based in New Zealand.

Australian Federal Police said they began investigating the 42-year-old in June, when he flew from the Gold Coast to Auckland.

"Over a two-week period, the man allegedly contacted electoral offices in NSW [New South Wales], Queensland and Tasmania on multiple occasions and made threats of self-harm and harming others," they said.

Police in New Zealand said they arrested the "Australian national" in Auckland after being notified of the allegations against him by their Trans-Tasman counterparts on 26 June.

Acting Senior Sergeant Craig Burrow, of Auckland City's Criminal Investigation Branch, said the calls were of an "offensive and threatening nature to the electorate office of an Australian federal and state member of Parliament".

The man was convicted of offensive use of a telephone in the Auckland District Court on 19 August, Burrow said.

The next day, he was arrested again - this time at Sydney Airport, after flying back from New Zealand. Australian police said they seized two mobile phones, books, and a passport.

He appeared before the New South Wales Bail Division Court the following day, facing one charge of using a carriage service to make a threat to cause serious harm and three counts of using a carriage service to menace, harass or cause offence.

He was refused bail and is due to appear at NSW's Downing Centre Local Court in October.

Immigration NZ would not confirm whether the man was on its radar at any point during his visit, or whether he remained in Auckland during the two months he was here, saying it would need a privacy waiver from him to comment on the case.

Australian Police also declined to provide further information, saying the matter was before the courts.

World.title: Blaze at cafe next to New Zealand's oldest building 'suspicious', FENZ says
World.content:
A fire at a cafe next to New Zealand's oldest surviving building is being investigated as suspicious.

Flames broke out at the back of the Honey House Café in Kerikeri overnight, a spokesperson for the cafe said on Saturday morning.

The business is next to Kemp House, which was built between 1821 and 1822 by missionaries, and was an important focus for early relationships between Māori and Pākehā.

Another heritage building, the Stone Store, which was built not much later - from 1832 to 1836, is also next door to the cafe.

The fire had been small, and "both Kemp House and Stone Store were thankfully unaffected by the blaze," the Honey House Café spokesperson said.

"Authorities are currently investigating, so the site is closed until further notice."

Fire and Emergency NZ (FENZ) said they were notified of the fire at 11:30pm Friday, and five crews responded.

The fire was "well involved" when firefighters arrived, and is being considered suspicious, they said, referring further enquiries to police.

Police said they were notified by FENZ of a fire on KeriKeri Road shortly before 1am on Saturday. A scene guard was then posted at the site overnight.

Police and a FENZ fire investigator would be at the scene on Saturday, looking into what caused the fire.

Re-roofing work is currently being carried out at Kemp House, with the aim to have it finished by summer.

World.title: South Africa rugby flyover controversy: How the Springboks' stadium tradition began
World.content:
It took only seconds for two jets to fly over DHL Stadium in Cape Town. It has taken considerably longer for them to fly out of the headlines.

Minutes before kick-off in the second test of the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series between the All Blacks and South Africa, two Airlink Embraer jets flew over the Stadium in formation, passing hair-raisingly close to the roof as fireworks erupted below.

Footage of the flyover quickly spread around the world, with flight-tracking data indicating one of the aircraft came within 12-14 metres of the stadium roof.

For those inside the stadium, it was a spectacular sight. For others, it was a moment of alarm.

All Blacks assistant coach Jason Ryan was among those caught off guard.

"I thought it was coming through the box," he said after the All Blacks' 33-26 loss to South Africa. "That was low. I don't know if it's a competition, but that's probably enough."

The spectacle has since prompted a different kind of scrutiny. South Africa's Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) started compliance checks and is examining flight data and other information relating to the flyover.

Airlink, meanwhile, has defended the operation. In a statement, the airline said flight data recorded by both planes confirms they were within the SACAA's approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast.

However, a planned flyover for Sunday morning's (NZT) third test of the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour at Johannesburg's FNB Stadium has since been scrapped, with Airlink citing unfavourable weather conditions.

So why does South African rugby have such an enduring fascination with stadium flyovers in the first place?

The answer lies in one of the most famous moments in the history of the Springboks - and in a country that was trying to redefine itself.

A tradition takes flight

On 24 June 1995, South Africa hosted New Zealand in the Rugby World Cup final at Ellis Park in Johannesburg.

It was far more than a rugby match.

South Africa had only recently emerged from apartheid and returned to international sporting competition after years of isolation. Nelson Mandela, elected president the previous year, had embraced the Springboks - once deeply associated with white Afrikaner nationalism - as a vehicle for reconciliation.

Mandela arrived at packed-out Ellis Park wearing a Springbok jersey. The nation was watching. Then came the roar.

South African Airways captain Laurie Kay piloted a Boeing 747-200 over the stadium, with the words "GOOD LUCK BOKKE" emblazoned across the underside of the wings. The aircraft made two passes, with the second lower and more dramatic than the first.

The image became inseparable from the mythology of that day: Mandela, Francois Pienaar, Joel Stransky securing the 15-12 victory with a drop goal - and, above them all, a jumbo jet announcing the occasion to the entire stadium.

The 1995 Rugby World Cup flyover at Ellis Park. ©INPHO/Billy Stickland

The 2009 film Invictus, which dramatised the events surrounding the 1995 World Cup, recognised the cinematic power of the moment and recreated the flyover for the big screen.

Since then, aircraft have become a familiar part of major Springbok matchdays. It has also become an opportunity for spectacle.

Masters of the mind games, the Boks used the tradition to machiavellian effect in 2024, timing the flyover just as the All Blacks' haka was reaching its crescendo.

The arrival of the Emirates Airlines A380 jumbo jet coincided with an explosion of fireworks and music, drowning out Kapa O Pango.

All Black Damian McKenzie voiced his displeasure about the tactic following New Zealand's 31-27 loss.

"I don't know when the plane was supposed to fly over. But it's an opportunity for us to connect with back home, we knew the noise was going to be there, but it's out of my control."

In 2024, an Emirates A380 jumbo jet did a flyover of Ellis Park while the All Blacks were performing the haka. Catherine Kotze / www.photosport.nz

How low can they go?

Last weekend's flyover in Cape Town proved the most daring flyover to date.

The stunning images were quickly shared on social media, with awe soon turning unease.

From some angles, the jets appeared to skim the stadium roof, while one aircraft flew right through the pyrotechnics. The footage prompted international concern about the margin for error when aircraft are operating so close to a large structure and a crowd of more than 50,000 people.

The airline behind the Airlink released a statement saying that the flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude - around 150 knots.

"The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.

"The two aircraft were flown by highly-experienced crew, with each comprised of three senior captains operating in the roles of commander, co-pilot and safety/technical officer."

Airlink also added that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirms that the flights were performed within the SACAA's approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast.

The SACAA said it had "initiated compliance verifications" with Airlink and will examine the available data before reaching its conclusions.

World.title: Country Life: Daffodil Day fundraising a farmer's legacy
World.content:
Daisy Groves was apparently renowned for her green thumb.

At Marangai, a 1200-hectare sheep and beef farm near Tinui east of Masterton, there are reminders of her all around the garden.

Perhaps ironically - given her name - it's the daffodils she planted through the front paddock that are her most enduring legacy.

Each year, the bright yellow blooms are picked and gifted to the local Cancer Society to help raise funds.

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The tradition first started in the 1990s and has been carried on by the farm's current owners Pattie and Tony O'Boyle, owners of Marangai for close to 20 years.

"When we were negotiating to buy the farm, after some time ... we had negotiated to buy and the other party had negotiated to sell," Pattie told Country Life.

"And then the previous owner said, 'oh, hold on, one more thing'. And we were like, 'oh, no, what could this be?', and it was, would we agree to the Cancer volunteers still coming each year to pick the daffodils on the driveway, and we were like 'of course'."

Marangai's Tony and Pattie O'Boyle. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It's grown into more of a community effort over the years, with friends, family, neighbours and even co-workers coming to help with the picking shortly before the annual Daffodil Day appeal.

"When we get to take them in the morning there's a big group of women [who] will be based in there just off Villa Street and they'll be bunching them for the sale and distribution and they're all just so incredibly thankful and grateful for what we bring.

"We do our best to pick the freshest ones and the more yellow ones."

The daffodils can be found in the front paddock that the main driveway runs through - it's fairly steep. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

About a dozen helpers turned out for this year's picking event. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It was a great chance for Marangai's new farm manager to get more familiar with the property. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

There are about 11 varieties to choose from though, carpeting the steep paddock which the main driveway winds through up to the homestead.

Pattie normally tries to pick about 10 to 15 buckets - which can be filled with dozens, even hundreds of stems.

Buckets filled, it was time for a break back at the house. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The property is home to 11 varieties of daffodils. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

She'll also take a bucket to the previous owners, Daisy's son John Langdon, and his wife Glennis.

"They like to sort of have a reminder of, you know, their family's legacy here."

For Pattie - herself, formerly a Groves, though of no relation - it's a reminder of the caretaker role farming families play.

She described Daisy as an "avid gardener".

"Every corner of this farm she's touched something, planted something."

World.title: Country Life: Christchurch red zone plants on Michelin-starred menu
World.content:
Pink peppercorn trees, creeping juniper, miner's lettuce, blackboy peaches - Adam Harrison is constantly surprised by the bounty of Christchurch's red zone.

"It's crazy the things we have over here that people just wouldn't expect."

The head chef of Michelin-starred and Cuisine-hatted restaurant Tussock Hill knows his way around it well - he's foraged from it for years.

Tussock Hill head chef Adam Harrison. Copyright 2025. All rights reserved.

From red zone to restaurant Country Life Download MP3 20m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The red zone refers to patches of suburban land throughout Christchurch which were damaged and deemed unsuitable for housing following the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes.

Shannon Dwyer (left) and Adam Harrison enjoy a walk through the red zone - and gather some produce along the way. RNZ/Anisha Satya

On the edge of Richmond, where blocks of houses once stood, only green grass and backyard plants remain.

But those plants, a reflection of the individuals who lived there, are now a diverse buffet for foragers - when you know where to look.

At the early end of spring, there's "a lot of green and not a lot of colour", Harrison said, but still plenty to forage.

On his walk around the red zone with Country Life, he foraged onion weed, juniper berries and branches, and tapped birch trees for their sap.

A basket of foraged onion weed and juniper from the red zone, destined for plates at the Tussock Hill Cellar Door Restaurant. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"Maple syrup is largely made up of sucrose and glucose.

"The birch syrup is slightly different. It's made up of fructose and glucose.

"The flavour we get in the end is more like a, sort of, balsamic vinegar, caramel, molasses."

Inner-city foraging is varied and concentrated. In the outer areas of Canterbury, foraged foods are abundant.

"There's a lot of coastal plants - ice plant, there's beach spinach, there's beach mustard.

"When we go out into North Canterbury, all the wilding apples that grow at the roadsides around the farms, we do a big forage sort of in autumn - last year we got 100 kilograms of apples."

Harrison's interest in foraging began in the rural English countryside, picking blackberries for pies or elderberries for cough syrup with his grandparents.

Adam Harrison and Shannon Dwyer harvest some magnolia flowers from a tree that borders the red zone. RNZ/Anisha Satya

He hopes to pass that curiosity on to diners when they taste foraged ingredients in Tussock Hill's food.

"The onion weed's a particularly interesting one because most people either have it in the garden, or see it in Hagley Park, and they'll probably just walk past it [or] over it.

An oxtail terrine with syrah jelly. Juniper berries, bone marrow custard and onion weed flowers adorn the plate, and juniper fronds are added for presentation. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"I hope next time they walk past it, they go, 'oh yeah, remember that? We had it at Tussock Hill'.

"For me, it's creating memories from something that's around you every day."

Both the foraged ingredients and produce grown on Tussock Hill's farm contributed to the restaurant's recent awards, Harrison said.

"We've put that story out there that we forage, we grow [our] own produce in the garden, we grow [our] own grapes, and what we've made as an experience is what we've been awarded for."

World.title: Mum left stranded with baby after British Airways refuses boarding for mistake it admits
World.content:
It's a parent's nightmare - being stranded unexpectedly at an airport with a small child.

Fleur Lonsdale was travelling in late May with her son, Oakley, one, from New Zealand, where she lives, to Europe for her mum's birthday.

After flying to Auckland Airport, she arrived at the check-in counter three hours early for her next flight to Geneva.

But she missed it after being told her son couldn't board because of a mistake on his ticket - a mistake she had been assured wouldn't matter by the airline.

"I've been in some fairly stressful situations, you know, I've worked for the military. I've worked with some very high-level people - and that had to be one that had to top some of them," she said.

Three months earlier, in February, Lonsdale had booked her flights on British Airways' (BA) website. Her one-year-old would be travelling on her lap for free but he needed his own ticket.

However, the ticket that had been generated looked strange, she said. Only the first letter of his name and four of his surname appeared.

Lonsdale was sure it wasn't her mistake.

"If that had been my mistake, then it would have been a one-letter mistake ... but there's no way that I would have put 'O' and then four letters of his last name."

She said she went to the company's online chat for help, in which an agent reassured her that this was a known system error and would not cause any problems with boarding.

However, when she made it to the airport, this turned out not to be the case.

BA declined to share the chat history or call logs with customer service with her, which Lonsdale is entitled to under the UK's General Data Protection Regulation laws.

RNZ has contacted its customer service and can confirm it records calls for monitoring and quality purposes.

In an email seen by RNZ from the airline to Lonsdale, BA appeared to admit fault for a system error which caused the misprint of her son's name.

"I also understand your frustration that the matter was ultimately acknowledged as stemming from a system-related issue rather than any error on your part," a customer service agent wrote to Lonsdale.

But when asked about this directly by RNZ, it did not provide an answer.

It also did not answer questions on whether such a system error was known about, or whether there were plans to fix it.

British Airways appeared to admit fault for the system error in an email seen by RNZ. AFP

The flight's operator, which was not British Airways, told Lonsdale she would need a form from British Airways to change her son's name to be allowed to board.

Lonsdale said she spent hours on the phone with British Airways' customer service, but nobody could help her.

She told RNZ that an agent left during the call to go home for the day.

"They've literally just kept me on hold, complete carelessness and just gone: 'Oh, well, I'm going to go home now. Screw this girl who's waiting at the airport with her one-year-old'."

Lonsdale said she was becoming increasingly distressed at missing her flight - and potentially her mum's birthday celebrations.

"It was just blame, blame, blame, your fault, your fault, your fault, you're going to have to pay for it."

Eventually, she broke down in tears, despite usually being calm, she said.

"I was just so shocked, I think. How is this even happening? Are you kidding me?

"Like I'm at the airport for a 35-hour flight with my one-year-old by myself and you're telling me that you can't get me on my flight when you told me you could?"

The agent then escalated the matter, and another told her they would book her on to a flight the next day.

She arrived in Europe a day late but in time for the party.

After complaining to the airline, and months of back-and-forth emails, it paid for the expenses incurred as a result of the delay, including accommodation for the extra night in Auckland and food.

It also provided compensation and a gift voucher, as a goodwill gesture.

But there was no mention of fixing the system error.

This prompted Lonsdale to share her story: she said she didn't want this to happen to another parent.

"This is about every mother who has to travel with her child. This should never be allowed to happen at any airline, not just them."

World.title: Nelson community 'shocked' by shooting
World.content:
A Nelson MP says the community is shocked after two people died in a shooting in the suburb of Tahunanui yesterday afternoon.

A man and a woman were found dead at a house on Parkers Road after a report of a shotgun being stolen in nearby Annesbrook.

Police say the two people were known to each other and they are investigating the circumstances of the deaths.

Acting Tasman District Commander Superintendent Blair Macdonald said it was an isolated incident and there was no ongoing threat to public safety.

However, Nelson MP Rachel Boyack says the seaside suburb isn't used to such incidents, and people are concerned.

Rachel Boyack is the MP for Nelson. Max Frethey / LDR

"People are reassured there's no risk to public safety but, you know, we have a really caring community and when these types of incidents occur people are really concerned about their friends, their family, their community," Boyack told RNZ.

"Our love and thoughts go to the family and friends of those involved," she wrote on Facebook.

World.title: Opals make winning start to World Cup campaign
World.content:
Australia's women's basketball team have begun their World Cup campaign in Germany with an entertaining 70-54 win over Puerto Rico.

The Opals were pushed throughout by their opponents in the Group C opener in Berlin.

Steph Talbot was superb for Australia, earning the player-of-the-game award after posting 19 points, eight rebounds and three assists.

Ezi Magbegor also reached double figures in scoring with 11 points and led the way on the boards with nine.

Alanna Smith starred with 10 points and eight rebounds but left the court during the game with what looked like a lower left-leg injury.

Jade Melbourne chipped in with 10 points, while Zitina Aokuso and Isobel Borlaise had six each to help get the job done on day one of competition.

Arella Guirantes (14 points), Trinity San Antonio (11) and Imani McGee-Stafford (11) were Puerto Rico's top scorers.

Ranked third in the world behind the USA and France, the Opals were unbeaten in qualifying and crowned Asia Cup champions in 2025.

They have won medals in three of the past four World Cups since winning gold in Brazil 20 years ago.

They claimed silver in Spain in 2018, as well as bronze in Türkiye four years earlier and again on home soil in 2022.

The Opals face world number 16 Türkiye on Sunday and fifth-ranked Belgium the following day.

AAP

World.title: What are the World Nomad Games and why are Australians competing?
World.content:
The horse is already moving when Sezim Jumabekova draws her bow.

She has three targets to hit before the track runs out.

She grips the horse with her thighs, twists at the waist, and shoots.

Ms Jumabekova, 29, from Kyrgyzstan, has been riding competitively for only three years.

"I've fallen off many times and torn my clothes learning new tricks," she said.

Sezim Jumabekova tries out new tricks ahead of the opening ceremony. (Supplied: Sezim Jumabekova)

Despite being a relative newcomer to the sport, she is competing in horseback archery in the World Nomad Games from August 31 to September 6 in Kyrgyzstan.

Kyrgyzstan launched the World Nomad Games in 2014 as a stage for the traditional sports and cultures of Central Asia's nomadic peoples.

What began with 20 countries and 10 traditional sports has grown, in just over a decade, into an international competition of about 100 countries competing across 43 events.

Repackaging heritage as sport

An eagle hunter, also known as berkutchi, competes. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

Some of the sports are obscure outside the region, like eagle and falcon hunting and Kok-boru, where a horseback team wrestles for a sheep.

"It's like AFL and the NRL here in Australia, but on horseback," said Ahmed Kharat, captain of the Australian team competing in archery events in this year's games.

Many of the sports have cultural significance and local audiences.

Eagle hunting on command traces back to the Mongol conquests of the 12th and 13th centuries.

Falconry is a traditional sport with hunting assisted by Taigan hounds. (Reuters: Pavel Mikheyev)

Other events trace a long lineage.

An 11-kilometre horse race is among some of the equestrian events that have a rich history in neighbouring Mongolia and Kazakhstan.

Another is Er enish, a traditional Kyrgyz horseback wrestling sport.

The team from Kazakhstan unseated opponents to win gold in both the 60-kilogram and 70-kilogram categories this year.

Two teams compete in Kok-Boru, throwing a stuffed sheepskin into a goal for points. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

There are several other competitions competed on foot.

One times how quickly teams put up a yurt, a traditional portable nomadic dwelling used by nomadic families moving between pastures.

In another event called Ordo, teams use sheep knucklebones to flick opposing pieces from a marked ring.

Eagle hunting dates back to the Mongol Empire days. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

From Soviet torpedo factories to Insta-stan famous

The World Nomad Games is more than entertainment.

Regional commentators also point to their political and economic purpose.

Kyrgyzstan is a young state, which became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991, building its national identity from its nomadic past.

It was deeply integrated into the Soviet industrial machine, with one of its largest factories producing torpedoes for the Soviet navy.

The 6th World Nomad Games kicked off this week in Kyrgyzstan. (Reuters: Pavel Mikheyev)

When the Soviet Union collapsed, so did those jobs.

"Kyrgyzstan is quite unique as it experienced a lot of outward migration to the countryside after the collapse," said Kiril Nourzhanov, an associate professor in Central Asian Studies at the Australian National University.

"The economy of Kyrgyzstan was hit for six, and it experienced deindustrialisation, so more people began to engage in agriculture, including the traditional nomadic pastoralism," he added.

A service economy has emerged in the gap, and tourism now ranks among the country's most valuable sectors.

Tourism has soared in recent years, with tour companies such as Intrepid Travel reporting a 900 per cent increase in bookings to Kyrgyzstan this year compared to last year.

Delegates from Russia and Iran attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan this week. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

Gulshat Rozyyeva, a research scholar from the Australian National University's Centre for Arab and Islamic Studies, called the Games "a major identity booster".

She said it was an opportunity for Kyrgyzstan to appear as more than "one of Central Asia's poor countries".

"It doesn't have the natural resources like Kazakhstan or Turkmenistan," she said.

"But it has mountains, and a horse culture, and so the World Nomad Games are important economically, too, as people book hotels, and support local businesses."

Horse tricks were performed during the opening ceremony. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

The Kyrgyz government has invested heavily in that image: horses grazing on a backdrop of snow-capped mountains and pristine blue lakes.

This year the World Nomad Games double as a diplomatic stage, hosting delegates from Russia, Iran, India, and China at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan's capital, Bishkek.

Ms Rozyyeva said the balancing act was a familiar one for Kyrgyzstan — asserting a distinct national identity while leaning economically on its larger neighbours.

China invests in infrastructure in the country under the Belt and Road Initiative, while migrant workers in Russia send remittances back home to Kyrgyzstan.

A digital revival of an analogue culture

Ms Jumabekova grew up in Bishkek, far from the high mountain pastures traditionally associated with the country's nomadic culture.

She was teased for being a city girl, but was drawn to learning about horses and became a guide leading horseback tours, learning acrobatics and trick riding.

She said she was passionate about rediscovering skills from semi-nomadic life.

"Nowadays young people are interested in the digital world," she told the ABC.

"Each year it gets harder to save our nomad culture, perhaps because it brings in less money."

Participants from the UK take part in a tug-of-war competition. (Reuters:Pavel Mikheyev)

The irony is that the digital world and Instagram videos from tourists may also be helping preserve it.

Australian archer Daniya Aziz, 23, said that these sports haven't just seen a revitalisation in Central Asia.

"I think in the age that we are in, because we're so social media heavy, so technologically dependent, there has been … an urge to sort of disconnect from that," she said.

"There's no better way to do that than through these cultural sports because they have that element of physicality and an element of being outdoors.

Speed yurt assembly is one of the more traditional sports in the games. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

" It's a really nice way for us, from diverse backgrounds in Australia, to connect back to that culture identity. "

Ms Aziz said she was attracted to horseback archery for its challenge.

When contestants arrive in Kyrgyzstan, they pick sticks from a hat as part of a lottery and are allocated a horse at random.

"What's really cool about horseback archery is that it's building that connection between horse and archer so that when you are going down a track, you're going down as one unit," she said.

Kyrgyz archer Asel Sadyrova believes these sports also promote aspirations for girls today, building strength and confidence while keeping alive history that may otherwise be forgotten.

Asel Sadyrova is teaching girls in Kyrgyzstan traditional wooden bow archery. (Supplied: Asel Sadyrova)

"Epics and tales passed down preserve our nation, and my grandfather's stories about heroic, courageous women who defend their people from enemies make me remember we are the heroines of the modern age," she said.

"I believe young people want to follow in the footsteps of these heroines."

World.title: Sabalenka interrupts US Open match over cannabis smell
World.content:
Aryna Sabalenka had an unusual interruption during her US Open third-round match, stopping play to ​alert the umpire to a strong smell of cannabis drifting onto Louis Armstrong Stadium court.

The world number one, who secured a 6-3, 6-4 win against Uzbekistan's Kamilla Rakhimova, ​raised the issue during her ‌second service game, pointing out the smell before play resumed.

"Someone is smoking weed," top seed Sabalenka told umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore as she was serving 30-0 up.

"Do you mind? Because it's ‌so strong."

Sabalenka later told reporters she was not objecting to anyone enjoying themselves but pleaded for the smoking to be kept away from the ‌court.

"I was like, 'Guys, you can ​do whatever, you can ‌smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please not do it around the tennis courts,'" a smiling Sabalenka said.

"It's a bit tricky to handle that smell while you're trying to compete at your best."

The odour of ​cannabis ‌has become a familiar — if unwelcome — feature at Flushing Meadows, with players complaining about the distraction in the past.

While smoking is not permitted inside the grounds, ⁠recreational cannabis is legal for adults over ‌21 in New York.

Smoke from people in the surrounding Flushing Meadows-Corona Park can drift into the tennis complex and ‌on to the courts.

Sabalenka said she had previously smelled cannabis at the tournament but never so strongly during a match, with the wind ‌apparently ​carrying the odour into ⁠the stadium.

"I don't know if it was coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium," she said.

"I just hope they ⁠are a bit more aware of that stuff."

As her post-match media conference continued, Sabalenka laughed when questions returned to the subject.

"Come ‌on, guys. I ‌think there is nothing else to say about weed," she said.

"I'm just ​asking people not to smoke it next to the tennis court."

Pegula advances to fourth round

Jessica Pegula rallied from behind to beat fellow ​former US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez 1-6, 6-4, 6-3 and make the fourth round.

Third seed Pegula faces Sorana Cîrstea in the last 16 and will need to iron out some of the flaws in ​her game after a sluggish ‌start against Fernandez.

But the American showed the resilience and composure that have made her one of the title contenders.

Back at Arthur Ashe Stadium, where her dream run ended against Emma Raducanu in ‌the 2021 final, Fernandez seized the initiative and rarely allowed Pegula ⁠to find any rhythm early in the contest.

Jessica Pegula moved through to the fourth round after defeating Leylah Fernandez. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

"It was really tough ‌today. I always feel it's hard ​to play her. I ‌never feel comfortable when I play her, even when I have won," said Pegula, who was the 2024 US Open runner-up.

"I was going to have to dig deep. I'm glad I was able to find somewhere there in the second set to turn it around.

"She's a great player, so ​it ‌was really hard. A lot of it revolves around my serve. My serve percentage was pretty bad."

Romanian 16th seed Cîrstea, 36, extended her impressive farewell-season campaign with ‌a ​clinical 6-3, 6-3 win over ⁠Italy's 19th-seeded Jasmine Paolini.

Ukraine's ‌Marta Kostyuk, seeded 11th in New York, advanced to the fourth round with a straight-sets 6-3, 6-2 victory over Russian ‌Ekaterina Alexandrova.

In the men's draw, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz underlined his status as the player to beat with a ruthless 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 victory over China's Wu Yibing.

The victory extended Alcaraz's match-winning streak at the majors to 17 following his triumph at Flushing Meadows last year and his Australian Open ‌win in February.

The two-time US Open victor next faces American 20th seed Tommy Paul, who defeated 15th-seeded Alexander Bublik 6-4, 3-6, 6-7 (4/7), 6-1, 6-3.

Meanwhile, Russian seventh seed Daniil Medvedev overpowered Frenchman Arthur Rinderknech with a ​6-4, 6-4, 6-4 victory.

Reuters

World.title: Jai Arrow's last NRL game was the second of a lifetime
World.content:
The record books will show that Jai Arrow’s last game as a South Sydney Rabbitoh lasted exactly one second.

It was one second not for a career, but for a footballing life as rugby league gave him everything it could, which was everything it had.

This was one second that really mattered in a way a century of Rabbitohs-Roosters matches never could. Their hatred, which flared up later on, felt insignificant.

Normally the NRL defines and destroys itself according to such bitterness but for one second it felt so easy to stow away that pettiness. Never has so much been fit into that second.

There was room for Arrow to run onto the field, to wave to his wife Berina and his daughter Ayla Rae in scenes that summoned an emotion deeper than description can provide.

There was room for former Rabbitoh brothers-in-arms to line the tunnel to cheer him on, lustily and loud, just how he would have wanted it.

Some of them are still playing in the NRL now. Was it really just a year ago they last met Arrow under the bright lights?

South Sydney's rivalry with the Roosters was put aside for the night for Arrow. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

His last two weeks are Arrow’s bravest as he’s brought up his 99th and 100th game for South Sydney following his motor neurone disease (MND) diagnosis, but his final full season was certainly his toughest.

He carried a series of injuries through a rotten Bunnies campaign to earn a place of high honour in winning the club’s player of the year award, leading from the front in many a footballing battle that was lost long before kick-off.

Some of those who lined the tunnel left such fights behind many seasons ago, former teammates and greybeards alike, but they shared a desire to return to give their mate a send off nobody could have ever imagined he'd ever need.

All of them were there when it mattered to slap his back, to shout his name, to make him feel like the player he has always been and was again one last time.

The Rabbitohs ran out big winners in Arrow's final match. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

There was room for Arrow to walk on with hope in his heart and perhaps, just for a second, to hear the sweet, silver song of a lark as the emotion fell down upon him.

There was room for a moment with Cody Walker, who just last week Arrow begged to spray him as he left the field against Gold Coast so things could feel like they used to be.

The brotherhood between the two men was palpable and their embrace was proof deeds are truer than words and that while it’s easy to tell somebody you love them it’s more important, if you can, to try and show them.

There was room for an embrace with Wayne Bennett, who has done so much for so many men in his half century of coaching but has never had to grapple with something like this.

Last week he helped Arrow put his boots on. This week he just held him.

Arrow’s face had been fighting the tears since the moment he hit the lights of the stadium and they welled up when he met Walker but only when he found Bennett’s arms did they flow, nakedly and unashamed, before his coach held his hand and led him to his family.

Arrow's journey has led to an outpouring of emotion across rugby league. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

He sat on the bench for the final 79 minutes and 58 seconds, wrapped in a coat and chatting to Souths players about nothing and everything as he became a footballer for one more second, a second the game will carry forever.

Sport often drifts towards self-importance but this is a case where it can be actually important.

For proof of that rest assured that result of the match, which the Rabbitohs won 50-20, did not mean all that much.

It was a fine enough way to spend a Friday evening. A lot of things happened therein, from tries to bizarre refereeing calls to a face off between Keaon Koloamatangi and Spencer Leniu that Arrow would have loved, especially since South Sydney got the better of it.

None of it mattered as much as the first second, a second that had to happen now if it was to happen at all.

Arrow’s degeneration since his public revelation of his diagnosis in May is already plain to see, even as there is no doubt he will continue on as bravely as a person can.

There is no known cure for motor neurone disease. Even with the assurance that anything that can be done for Arrow will be done, the hardest of days loom.

But on Friday night, there was still some time.

Time for an ancient rivalry to seem small as it was postponed for something that really mattered.

Time for men, some of whom might not know their emotions all that well, to embrace as brothers and bear their hearts to one another, bleeding and raw and full.

Time to feel the love and to show it, to share the things we too often do not say.

Time for the sport that has been such a part of Arrow’s life to give him the greatest gift it could muster, all wrapped up in just one second.

World.title: Adelaide returns to scene of finals flop to face biggest test of growth
World.content:
Every week it seems like there is history being written in the AFL.

Some of this is welcomed, memorable and celebrated, such as when Scott Pendlebury broke the games record earlier this year, or when Lance Franklin notched the 1,000-goal mark in 2022.

Moments like these are cherished throughout each club's fanbase and reflects the long history of the league and sport.

Other slices of history are far more trivial. Last week, Sam Walsh set the record for the most disposals in the Wildcard Finals round. While the stat is interesting, it is not necessarily illustrative of a feat of great importance.

Nonetheless, it provides colour to the rich tapestry that is Australian football.

Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks is hoping to avoid an unwanted slice of history this weekend. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

And there are some feats that players and coaches avoid like the plague.

Many football fans know the tale of Kevin Murray. The former Roys stalwart managed to play 333 games, all without winning a single final — a league record.

While his career was rich and storied, eventually earning him Legend status in the Hall of Fame, the achievement underscored the futility of playing for Fitzroy through most of the second half of the 20th century.

Though never winning a VFL final, Murray did manage to play in a finals win during a lucrative mid-career stint at East Perth in 1966 on the way to a losing Grand Final against Perth.

This Saturday night Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks is set to, at least temporarily, claim his own slice of footballing ignominy.

Nicks will join Alec Hall as the coaches to steer their sides through the most VFL/AFL games without winning a final.

For those who don't immediately recognise the name Alec Hall, his last game as coach came more than a century ago.

Over the last two years Nicks's Crows have won the second most regular season games. Last year's minor premiership season was cut short with a straight sets exit.

This year the Crows are already on their last chance with a rampaging Bulldogs ahead of them.

Nicks has quietly rebuilt his side's biggest question mark. But in the Bulldogs, the Crows face a test designed to test this weakness in full.

Mayhem in the middle

The Crows midfield was bossed by Jai Newcombe and Hawthorn in last year's semifinal loss at home. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed)

Fresh in the mind of Nicks, and all Crows fans, is how their 2025 season came to an end.

Like all sides who fall short of their end goal, reflection on their failings quickly sets in.

For Nicks, the message on what went wrong was clear, and last year's disappointment has put them in a stronger place for this year.

"I think we're ahead of last year," Nicks said after their round 24 win over the Giants, despite being "a little lower on the ladder."

"We've been doing a lot of work around what it was we didn't get right last year. Under that immense pressure that Collingwood and Hawthorn brought last year we weren't able to execute and deliver our game on our game plan."

That pressure around the contest is arguably what brought their once-promising 2025 season undone. Against Hawthorn, the Crows struggled both at contests both at stoppage and in general play, with the Hawks midfield unit gaining control of the game.

Starved of opportunity with ball in hand, the Crows' defence could only do so much to hold the wave of Hawks back.

The Hawks ended that final with a six-clearance advantage and 20 more post-clearance ground ball gets. Starved of the ball, the Crows were left passengers in a finals series that they were meant to drive from the front.

At the most basic level, only part of the contest game needed adjustment from the outside. The Crows finished the 2025 season leading for post-clearance ground ball gets and contested possessions.

They were relatively weak at stoppage, however, with a negative clearance differential across the year.

But that hid a slide against the best of the best.

The Crows struggled more against good opposition midfields than most other contenders, perhaps the canary in the coalmine for their finals struggles.

This is despite their units at either end of the ground largely holding up their ends of the bargain.

The Crows defence in 2025 and 2026 has actually gotten stronger against the best sides in the league. They conceded just 1.47 points per inside 50 this year — better than any team's full season record.

The figures were even starker last year. While the Crows concede more in games against good sides, this has largely been down to an increased volume of inside 50s their defence has to protect against.

It's yet another mark of honour for the severely underrated Adelaide backline. Over the past two years the Crows defence has arguably been the strongest defensive unit in the league, despite the lack of individual acknowledgement.

Only one Crows defender, Wayne Milera, has made the All-Australian team in this time despite the depth and strength of their taller options.

While their forward line has had a rotating list of players contribute it has been a little stronger when it matters most.

The territory battle at the contest, particularly up the ground and at stoppage, is so important for one of the Crows' other weaknesses.

Despite their defensive miserliness, their backline has struggled to transition the ball from defensive 50 and the defensive half to create scoring opportunities.

It means the Crows can absorb the pressure of opposition attacks, but sometimes struggle to get the game back on their terms in this way.

Without the benefit of winning the territory battle, or control of the footy at the contest, it can make a spellbinding side look pedestrian at best.

The shift

Izak Rankine has had an excellent season after missing last year's finals through a self-inflicted suspension. (AAP: Matt Turner)

This has spurred the Adelaide brains trust into action. Throughout this year Nicks has experimented with different looks up the ground.

Bodies have floated through the middle and up forward to try to execute when it matters most.

The highest profile change through the year was one involving a player who missed last year's finals altogether.

Since he entered the league with Gold Coast, Izak Rankine has long been viewed as one of the game's most damaging attacking players. He is the type of player that makes the hair stand up on the back of your neck, or your eyes quickly dart back to the TV if the commentator mentions his name in excited tones.

His 2025 season ended not due to form or injury, but rather as a consequence of using a homophobic slur towards a Collingwood player in round 23. Suspended for four matches, Rankine admitted his mistake and apologised publicly and privately.

It is always difficult to judge atonement and sincerity from a distance, but Rankine has made further efforts to build a relationship with the Rainbow Crows supporter group, which has in turn praised the progress made.

Some fans, both of Adelaide and the sport more broadly, may need more time to evaluate his response to the incident.

Others, particularly a large cohort of Crows fans, believed the punishment to be too severe from the outset.

Regardless of your stance, Rankine appears to be choosing his own course in making amends for his grave misstep.

AFL bans Rankine for four games over 'highly offensive' homophobic slur Adelaide Crows star Izak Rankine has been suspended for four matches for using a homophobic slur against a Collingwood opponent during last weekend's AFL match at Adelaide Oval.

Rankine's on field evolution in 2026 is far easier to evaluate than anything off field.

This year Rankine has been deployed full time in the middle of the ground for the first time in his career. The results have been dramatic.

Since the shift, Rankine has been about the most damaging player in the competition, with his previous skill in limited opportunities scaling up when foisted around the ball more often.

The tipping point for Nicks to throw Rankine through the middle more was making sure the young Crow fit with the defence first mindset of the side.

"I've always wanted to play midfield." Rankine told AFC.com.au earlier this month.

"I just had to fix up my two-way running, understanding the game, and when the opposition gets momentum against us how to mentally stay in the game and not get frustrated.

"I've found that the way I can get more of those opportunities is really delving into the defensive side of the game, getting back and helping the defenders, and being an option for them when they get stuck."

It's hard to overstate the growth in Rankine's game. Rankine has moved his predominantly front-half game to impact across the ground.

Defensively, Rankine has increasingly involved himself at contest and tracked his opponent while retaining that attacking flair that makes his game so appealing.

In that time, Adelaide has become even stronger at the contest without suffering on the defensive side. Rankine provides an explosive attacking strength that few other sides can boast, and his improved defensive effort has cost the Crows little the other way.

Rankine is not the only adjustment the Crows have made in the middle through the year.

The Crows have exposed players like Jake Soligo and Brayden Cook at the contest, with other experiments along the way. Instead of direct results on a week to week basis, it appears that Nicks is attempting to expose a wider group to action in the middle in order to maximise his options come September.

Perhaps the last shift might be their biggest, as over the past month the Crows have shifted recent draftee Dan Curtin to the guts in order to provide a vastly different look.

At 197cm and with the build of a key position player, Curtin may be the league's biggest full-time midfielder.

If it sticks, Curtin might provide a midfield option that few other sides have seen before.

Daniel Curtin has averaged a career-best 15.5 disposals per game this season. (Getty Images: James Elsby)

"He's still got so much upside in his game. We haven't really scratched the surface there yet," Nicks said.

"I think we see Dan as a midfielder moving forward. We feel like he's got the football intelligence, the execution and the awareness that you need to be a midfielder.

"He's unique in that he's such a big body, so he's a tough match-up. He's still a very young player that's still learning a fair bit about the game. But it's exciting for us."

Curtin presents opponents a rare challenge of raw size alongside unquestioned footballing ability, similar to Patrick Cripps and experiments with ruck-mids such as Mark Blicavs and Luke Jackson.

Curtin's exposure to different roles across his short professional career has also gifted him with a sense of defensive responsibility when running through the middle — key to executing the Crows' game plan.

A meeting with the biggest midfield test

Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli (pictured) and teammate Ed Richards present a challenge to Adelaide's midfield. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Given how much of their focus has been on building their game at the contest, it is somewhat fitting that their first finals test comes against arguably the league's most damaging contested side on their day.

While the Bulldogs are entering September with a depleted forward line and a defence with more questions than answers, few can question the raw ability and system of their midfield unit.

For a side entrenched in the mid-table hustle over the last two years the Dogs are a side few want to see when the footy starts to get serious.

It's that ability in the middle of the ground, led by All-Australian duo Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards, that is set to stress test Nicks's personnel changes.

While the Crows have improved their work at the contest as the year has progressed, the results across the whole year paint a similar picture to that of 2025.

Looking at the entire season likely undersells where they sit right now. While they lost the clearance battle to Fremantle in round 23, they dominated the post-clearance contested battle — crucial to maintaining field position.

Despite Adelaide's strong performances over the last two years, rumbling from Victoria has suggested that Nicks must steer the Crows to victory to retain his job.

"I understand the narrative, it's part of this industry, [but] it's probably not something I could talk to," Nicks said.

If, for whatever reason, the Crows do the unthinkable and remove Nicks from his post after the season, it would be a move without little recent precedent.

The most recent coach to lead his side to at least 33 wins over his last two seasons in charge before leaving his role was Mick Malthouse in his "negotiated handover" to Nathan Buckley at Collingwood.

Few, if any, coaches have been legitimately sacked in league history with so many home and away wins immediately prior to their removal.

While it is likely just a rumour spread wild, the game on Saturday night presents a chance to silence the speculation of the doubters.

World.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional 100th Souths appearance, Souths thrash Roosters
World.content:
Tears flowed as Jai Arrow made his 100th Rabbitohs appearance, with his Souths teammates helping crush the reserve team of their arch rivals, the Roosters.

Arrow choked back tears when he was hugged by Wayne Bennett as the forward was given a hero's reception at a sold out Sydney Football Stadium.

The 31-year-old father of one was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) this year and, until two weeks ago, was stranded on 98 NRL games for the Bunnies.

At Bennett's initiative, the NRL allowed Souths an extra interchange against the Gold Coast last week for game number 99 and again on Friday against the Roosters.

"It was pretty emotional," Cam Murray told Channel 9.

"I'm just so happy that everyone was able to get around him and he's been able to feel all the love.

"I know he really appreciates it and we love to see it.

"We all love him and happy he was able to notch up 100 games."

Arrow led his teammates out to the sound of the Gerry and the Pacemakers rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone, with 14th Immortal and dual-club legend Ron Coote ringing the Rabbitohs' bell.

The former Queensland State of Origin forward was given a guard of honour by more than 100 Souths old boys, including members of the 2021 grand final squad Arrow was a member of and his family, who all sobbed along with him and plenty of others in the stands.

"It was emotional," Roosters captain Connor Watson said in his post-match press conference.

"It was very touching. Things like that are bigger than rugby league."

Jai Arrow presented a stong face to the Rabbitohs crowd. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

In the subsequent match, the Rabbitohs ran in 10 tries to pummel the Roosters 50-20, who had rested 10 of their star players with a top four spot secure.

But in completing the win, Souths have themselves earned a home finals spot, and will face Newcastle at either the Olympic Stadium or Sydney Football Stadium next week.

Campbell Graham scored twice for the Rabbitohs, who had nine different try scorers on the night, including Alex Johnston, who crossed for the 30th time this season.

Latrell Mitchell was one of them, scoring on his return to the starting line up while mixing his sublime skill with fearsome physicality, most notably when he flattened Toby Rodwell in the closing stages, standing over the stricken half like Mohammed Ali over Sonny Liston in their 1965 rematch.

If Mitchell's performance was heartening — a poor 5/10 kicking rate aside — Roosters firebrand Spencer Leniu will have raised concerns from coach Trent Robinson in the first half.

Leniu squared up to Keaon Koloamatangi after the Rabbitohs prop smashed him in a tackle twice in the same set, the second time tossing the ball away and giving away a penalty.

Titans fume over questionable calls

Earlier, the Dolphins hung on to beat the Titans 24-20 on the Gold Coast.

It was the Dolphins' seventh-consecutive win, but almost didn't happen as the Titans fought back late on and were unfortunate not to come away with the win.

The Titans were left fuming when, while leading 14-0, they had Keano Kini sin-binned in the 23rd minute for a very soft push on Dolphins winger Tevita Naufahu.

Josh Hannay was fuming after that call, and a trio of others in the closing minutes, went against his side.

"I thought it was incredibly harsh and not long after that they get a try from a knock-on," Hannay said.

"You talk about momentum swings — they don't get much bigger than that. Moe [Moeaki Fotuaika] got smacked in the face at the end and ends up in the bin for retaliating.

"[Jamayne Isaako] throws a leg out to trip [AJ Brimson] in the act of a potential try-scoring play and it is just a penalty.

"It was probably more sin-binnable than Keano's play.

"You stack all those things up and you lose by four points, you have got to be proud of your team's effort."

With AAP

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: 'Pat at his best': Cats skipper praised after elimination final win
World.content:
Geelong has ended Carlton's fairytale season with a solid win, after withstanding an early challenge to run away with their elimination final.

In the first finals meeting of the two teams since the 1995 grand final, Carlton got the early jump but could not keep control, as Geelong secured the win by 33 points on a rainy night at the MCG.

Geelong skipper Patrick Dangerfield led the way with five goals in his 378th AFL game.

Cats coach Chris Scott said Dangerfield stood tall when it counted.

"Late, [Dangerfield] was just so impressive," Scott said.

"It also wasn't as if he was bullying inexperienced players. He looked like Pat at his best."

The loss ended Carlton's season after a monumental run of 12 wins and a draw out of 16 games to get to the elimination final under new permanent coach Josh Fraser.

Geelong will travel to Perth to face Fremantle next week in a cut-throat semifinal.

Look back at how the action unfolded in the live blog below.

World.title: Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Aussie's EPL teen dream
World.content:
Lucas Herrington has gone to number one with a bullet in 2026, at a speed so dizzying it would leave many teenagers' heads spinning.

Turning 19 this weekend, he is fresh off a breakthrough World Cup, has a multi-million-dollar contract in the best football league in the world, and has fans fawning over him.

But true to his persona on the pitch, the central defender is calm, level-headed and capable of tackling any challenge.

"My parents have always instilled that factor of humility in my life and having that humbleness to stay grounded and just to keep working hard," he told Australian media on a call from Hull.

"I'm always trying to get better. So I think it's always having that positive mindset that I've still got a lot of things to work on. And I'm not the finished product."

Herrington was one of Australia's best players throughout the recent World Cup. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Herrington made his bolt-from-the-blue Socceroos debut in March, which turned into a maiden World Cup appearance a few months later.

His impressive efforts in North America captured interest from some of the biggest clubs in the world including Barcelona and Liverpool.

But he settled on Hull City, newly promoted in the English Premier League, and a five-year deal for a transfer fee reportedly worth $33 million with add-ons, to become the most expensive Australian player ever.

Alessandro Circati recently joined that rich list with his transfer from Parma to Benfica.

Herrington with his manager, Buddy Farah, after signing his record deal with Hull City last month. (Supplied: Hull City)

The money is astronomical for an Australian footballer, and despite his down-to-earth nature, even Herrington was lured in by the EPL stereotype of fancy, fast cars.

"It's a nice car park. I do have a car right now; it's nice. I'm enjoying it," he laughed, almost sheepishly.

But when he speaks about his off-field highlights in his few weeks in England, the teenager goes back to keeping it real.

"Mum's here at the moment. She leaves soon, so I've just been exploring around with her," he said.

"So that's been really nice, some great quality time with her."

Advice from a legend

Herrington made his debut for the Tigers off the bench in their upset win over Manchester United.

"It was only a week and a couple of days from when I landed to that game against Man United," he said.

"Great moment for the city and for me personally, with my mum and my agent in the stands, it was a super proud moment for me.

"And it was a great match, very grateful for the opportunity to be there."

Herrington celebrated the Tigers' upset win over Manchester United to open their season. (Getty Images: Molly Darlington)

He was again used as a substitute in a win over Coventry, while he started the EFL Cup penalty shootout win against Stoke.

A strong show of confidence for the youngster, who is the only Australian in England's top flight.

"It's probably the best league in the world. So to be here at 18 is super special," he said.

"I've always wanted to play in the Premier League, so I'm very grateful for the opportunity from the coaching staff and the club to do so. And I've loved my first three or so weeks here.

"It's a league with the best players in the world, so to be up against them every week is really special and a great challenge for me as a young defender.

"It's just about trying to learn as much as possible from the older boys in the team and just try and take every game as a lesson."

And don't mistake his modesty for meekness; he knows he belongs.

A message reinforced by former Sweden international Zlatan Ibrahimović, who publicly supported Herrington after missing a penalty in the Socceroos' World Cup round of 32 shootout loss to Egypt.

Herrington received plenty of public support after Australia exited the World Cup. (Getty Images: Alex Slitz)

“This is just the beginning of your career," Ibrahimović said on Fox Sports USA's post-game analysis.

"You stepping up there, you show a lot of courage. Not everybody would do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here."

Ibrahimović made good on his promise and ended up calling the Queensland product himself.

"He just said, really don't fear anyone. I'm here for a reason, so just go enjoy," Herrington said.

Dreams do come true

Herrington's meteoric rise means he has not yet played for Australia in his home state.

Herrington is hoping to play in the Socceroos' upcoming friendlies against Brazil in Queensland. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Something the former Roar product hopes to do in the Socceroos' friendlies against Brazil later this month, in Townsville and Brisbane.

"It'd be a dream come true to play for the Socceroos in Brisbane," he said.

"Something that I've always wanted to do, and to play in front of hopefully a packed-out Suncorp would be a dream, and in front of my family and friends would be awesome."

And he is happy to be a role model for others.

"Just trying to be an inspiration for all the young Australians that there is really a pathway to the Premier League," he said.

"I think a lot of young footballers in Australia like me wake up at all hours in the morning to watch the Premier League.

"So hopefully I can make them proud, make Australia proud.

"Just to keep working hard, enjoy the process, and to have big dreams because dreams do come true."

Tech.title: Audacity 4 is a complete revamp of the ‘world’s most popular’ audio editor
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Audacity 4 has been in the works for some time, and had its own mini controversy last year when an unfortunate redesigned logo started making the rounds. The final version of the new icon isn’t nearly as bad as the early rendition that was circulating last October. But more importantly, all the promised improvements to the self-proclaimed “world’s most popular audio editing and recording app” are here, turning Audacity from a free and capable but extremely clunky audio editor into a powerful modern tool.

The biggest change is the move to a non-destructive editing workflow. That means you can trim a clip down, then recover the audio simply by dragging the edge of the clip back out if you change your mind. Clips can now overlap too, which means you can still paste in audio even if there isn’t enough space and adjust after, or just freely drag audio around the timeline. Previously, if you tried to drag a clip past another one in the timeline, it would just stop dead in its tracks. You’d instead have to cut and paste it to move it past any existing audio.

You can also split clips now to easily chop up and rearrange audio. The developers refreshed clip envelopes and the built-in effects, and added a home screen with revamped project organization. Audacity also got a dramatic facelift that brings it more in line with Muse’s other products like Muse Score and Audio.com, complete with customizable themes.

While Audacity has been a staple of many people’s toolkits since it debuted way back in 2000, it’s stayed stubbornly consistent in its design and layout as new features have been bolted on, sometimes clumsily. This big refresh to Audacity 4 brings it much closer to a modern digital audio workstation (DAW).

Tech.title: The White House is making arcade games racist
Tech.content:
is a policy reporter at The Verge covering surveillance, the Department of Homeland Security, and the tech-right.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The PR masterminds at the White House just released a series of vaguely policy-themed “arcade” games, some of which are racist — and modeled on real games whose copyright holders may not be too happy to be associated with the MAGA agenda.

The Tetris Company has already responded to “Build the Wall,” which is obviously modeled on the famous puzzle game. In the Trump administration’s game, the player has to stack interlocking shapes to stop a “zombie border siege” along the southern border. Aliens — the administration’s preferred term for noncitizens, and the subject of previous grotesque attempts at humor — run across the screen, trying to get to America before the gates are shut.

In a statement to The Verge, Tetris spokesperson Kerri Brusca clarified that the company wasn’t involved in the creation of Donald Trump’s game. “For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy. The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible,” Brusca said. “We are currently reviewing the matter.”

The various companies whose brands the White House ripped off to make and promote these games — including Sega, Nintendo, Xbox, and the Flappy Bird Foundation Group — did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Previously, the Trump administration has gotten in trouble for infringing on others’ copyrights. The Department of Homeland Security has had to delete some of its racist, fancam-esque posts after receiving DMCA takedown requests.

The purpose of Trump’s interminable memes, games, and other gimmicks is manifold: to drum up support for Trump’s policies, to entertain his groyper fans, and, of course, to troll the libs. (One game, “Rio Run,” is like snake, except the head of the snake is a Border Patrol agent who collects migrants as he moves across the screen. Ha ha, get it? The president is deporting people.) But the games also inadvertently highlight the administration’s policy failures, not to mention the hypocrisy of Trump’s agenda.

Trump’s efforts to build a wall through protected lands in the Southwest, including Big Bend National Park, has been met with mass opposition — even from Republicans in deep-red Texas who form a key part of the MAGA coalition.

Other games are similar reminders of how Trump’s policies are backfiring, even on the right.

There’s “Flappy Bill,” a play on Flappy Bird that involves getting a bald eagle to deliver a piece of legislation to the National Mall. Cute! Except the administration has rolled back protections under the Endangered Species Act, the landmark legislation that helped rescue bald eagles from the brink of extinction. The administration’s supposed revamping of the National Mall has also been unpopular.

In “Supply Line,” reminiscent of the game Tapper, you have to knock processed foods — those filled with additives, seed oils, and artificial colorings — off a conveyor belt before they get fed to schoolchildren. But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hasn’t managed to do any of that. Besides issuing a likely AI-drafted report for his Make America Healthy Again commission, RFK Jr.’s main role at HHS has been to roll back vaccine recommendations and food safety regulations. The administration’s gutting of the Food and Drug Administration made it harder to investigate the spread of cyclosporiasis, the so-called explosive diarrhea parasite, earlier this year.

If anything, these games serve as a great reminder that our well-being is a big joke to the president and the people who surround him.

Tech.title: GoPro says it’s still committed ‘to your collective stoke’
Tech.content:
To our GoPro community, fans and customers,

We understand there’s some concern about GoPro’s post-merger commitment to continue developing market leading cameras for consumers and professionals. Making amazing cameras for all of you is our core DNA and reason for being and that will never change! We’re fired up about what’s ahead for GoPro and want to share a little more about what our proposed merger with Starman means for our future.

Thanks to the improved financial strength this merger will provide, we’ll be in a much better position to innovate, invent and advance the future of consumer and professional content creation. And importantly, Starman shares our passion for the GoPro brand, developing market leading products and our commitment to your collective stoke.

We’ve accumulated more than 2500 patents over the last 24 years which tells you we’ve been busy innovating, and this merger will ensure we’re able to innovate for many more years to come. We expect this merger will make GoPro a stronger, more capable camera company than ever before.

Our goal is to become a more diversified company which can make us stronger financially, enabling GoPro to become as awesome as we (and you) want us to be. We plan to bring you more innovative cameras, smarter accessories, and more powerful software and services designed to make capturing, editing and sharing your experiences easier and more exciting than ever. We see opportunities to improve the products you already love while developing new tools and experiences that help you create, connect and share in entirely new ways.

We have so much more to do, so much more to invent, and so much more we want to bring to the GoPro community. We appreciate all of you who have been on this journey with us and we’re excited about where we’re headed. We’re going to keep doing what we do best - making the world’s highest-performance cameras and building the products, services and innovations that help you capture life’s most exciting moments. It’s what we were founded to do and it’s what we will always do. Be a HERO…GoPro.

With respect and appreciation — Nick

GoPro Founder & CEO

Tech.title: Roland is getting into generative AI music with Melody Flip
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

It’s not quite the “push button; get song” of Suno, but Roland’s new Melody Flip tool marks the company’s foray into generative AI music. Available as a plug-in for your digital audio workstation (DAW), Melody Flip offers around 250 “Palettes,” which are essentially themed collections of musical ideas sorted by genre. You can start from scratch and ask it to generate any combination of melody, chord progression, bassline, or drums. Or you can feed it a reference track and have it build off the melodic ideas from that.

Unlike Suno or Udio, Melody Flip doesn’t spit out fully polished songs with vocals and full arrangements. Instead, it offers simple musical loops meant to serve as a creative spark for you to build on. There are fairly limited control over the outputs. You can’t feed Melody Flip a text prompt like “acoustic country rock with clean male vocals, literate singer-songwriter, gentle brushed drums, and sparse pedal steel at 98BPM” and get a Jason Isbell ripoff. Instead, you basically just choose a genre, note density, BPM, musical key, and take what you get. Though the genre options are pretty fine-grained, going from standard fare like “80s disco” and “90s R&B” to esoteric things like “Kawaii Future Bass” and “Anime World.”

The sound selection is further proof that you’re not supposed to use Melody Flip outputs out of the box. The presets available are mostly the sort of general MIDI tones you’d find in ‘90s video games. It seems like the intended use is to export the MIDI data from Melody Flip directly into your DAW to manipulate and pair with other, more powerful synth plugins.
